kind: deep research — every factual claim of the chapter, web-verified by topic, each flagged claim challenged by an independent skeptic, then adjudicated in the main loop
method: Six topic researchers (T1 crow, T2 lion, T3 Mahābhārata verse, T4 Hitopadeśa and subhāṣita, T5 etymology, T6 forms) inventoried each claim in the fact base, the five lessons and chapter.md with exact quotes, verified it against primary texts and standard scholarship, and proposed exact fixes. Every non-verified claim went to a skeptic told to refute it. Upheld findings were applied in the main loop (the skeptic's better fixes where given), conflicts between topics were merged by hand, and the result was validated (scripts/validate.py 0/0).

claims.claim: The earliest known version is 'a short Greek epigram of the 1st century CE' (Bianor, Greek Anthology 9.272).
claims.evidence: Anthologia Palatina 9.272 is by Bianor (Perseus Greek Anthology, Paton vol. III, 1917, docAuthor 'Bianor'). It is six lines (three elegiac couplets): Καρφαλέος δίψει Φοίβου λάτρις … κρωσσίον ὀμβροδόκον … χερμάδα … λαοτίνακτον ὕδωρ. A bird 'parched with thirst', 'Phoebus' servant', sees a rain-catching pitcher on a woman's tomb, cannot reach the water, is given the craft by Phoebus, and drops pebbles until the water rises. Bianor of Bithynia was an epigrammatist of the Garland of Philip, active under Augustus and Tiberius, so 'of the 1st century CE' is right. Cherniss and Helmbold's Loeb note on Plutarch, De sollertia animalium 967A, cites it as 'Anth. Pal. ix. 272', and J.N. O'Sullivan discusses it in JHS 99 (1979) 165. The epigram names no species: 'Phoebus' servant' is Apollo's bird, usually the raven in Greek myth. Teachers should not say the Greek text says 'crow'.

claims.claim: "Its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin — a short Greek epigram of the 1st century CE, and the Latin verse fables of Avianus (c. 400 CE)" (restated in l01 Q8(b) and in fact 0.1).
claims.evidence: 'Greek and Latin' is right, but Avianus is not one of the earliest known versions. Several witnesses come long before Avianus (c. 400 CE). The Latin is Pliny, Natural History 10.125 (published 77 CE): 'tradendum putavere memoriae quidam, visum per sitim lapides congerentem in situlam monimenti …' The Greek are Plutarch, De sollertia animalium 10 (Moralia 967A, c. 100 CE), on the ravens of Libya (τῶν ἐν Λιβύῃ κοράκων) that, needing drink, throw in stones and raise the water until it is within reach, and Aelian, De natura animalium 2.48 (early 3rd c.), where Libyan ravens drop pebbles (ψήφους) into rooftop water jars. Mayhoff's apparatus at NH 10.125 and the Loeb Plutarch note list these parallels. So the two earliest known witnesses are Bianor's Greek epigram and Pliny's Latin report, both of the 1st century CE. Avianus, about 350 years later, is the ancient fable-collection telling with the moral the lesson quotes. Pairing a 1st-century epigram with a c. 400 CE poem as 'the earliest known versions' hides three centuries of earlier evidence. Pliny's report is the natural Latin partner (open item 1). Adding it needs the new key rackham1940; Avianus's moral and Bianor's epigram get duff1934 and paton1917.

claims.correct_wording: Its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin, both of the 1st century CE: a short Greek epigram (Bianor, Greek Anthology 9.272), and a report passed on by Pliny the Elder (Natural History 10.125) that a raven was seen dropping stones into an urn of rainwater on a tomb until the water rose within reach. The Latin verse fables of Avianus (c. 400 CE, Fabulae 27) tell it as a fable, with the moral that cleverness beats force. If no new key is added, the minimal accurate form is: 'Its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin: the oldest is a short Greek epigram of the 1st century CE, and the Latin verse fables of Avianus (c. 400 CE) tell it as a fable, with the moral that cleverness beats force.'

challenge.reason:
Upheld, but the fixes have to change. The original is wrong as written. It names a 1st-century Greek epigram and Avianus (c. 400 CE) as "the earliest known versions", and Q8(b) makes that the right answer. Pliny's Latin report (NH 10.125, 77 CE) is about 320 years older than Avianus. Plutarch (Moralia 967A, written after 70 CE) also comes before Avianus; he calls the Libyan-raven story a μῦθος, a tale. So does Aelian (NA 2.48, early 3rd c.). The lesson itself frames the question as "where the story is first written down", so Pliny counts. The course's own skeptic had already flagged this in research/evidence ("Avianus (c. 400 CE) is not a first appearance: Pliny (77 CE) ... earlier"), and the draft brought the error back.

The proposed wording is accurate in substance. I checked it against the primary texts: Bianor's poem, Pliny's raven (masculine forms, in his chapter on ravens) and Avianus 27 with its cleverness-over-force moral.

The fixes are not correct as given:
(1) The lesson fix adds Pliny to a HISTORY callout cited only to perry1952. That breaks EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES §2.1 and the lesson's own rule that a Pliny sentence needs rackham1940, which is not yet in REFERENCES.md.
(2) The notes fix cites four keys that REFERENCES.md does not have (paton1917, rackham1940, duff1934, piyusham5) and proposes no entries for them. piyusham5 belongs to a different claim (open item 3), and its locus is unverified ("chapter 10 or 16 depending on edition").
(3) The notes replacement repeats the Pliny sentence that follows it.
(4) It leaves stale metadata that contradicts the change: "Pliny sentence is **not used**", open item 1, the register audit, and the REF in the Q8 key.
(5) "Both of the 1st century CE" with exactly two items is too exclusive. The Loeb editors the researcher cites date Plutarch's dialogue after 70 CE, perhaps as early as Pliny, so the researcher's "c. 100 CE" is imprecise. "Among them" fixes this.

The better_fixes add rackham1940 to REFERENCES.md, cite it in the callout and the Q8 key, drop the unneeded and unverified keys, and update the metadata.

Dry run on a scratch copy (the repo was not edited): every quote occurs exactly once, and validate.py reports 0 errors in 61 lessons. Without the REFERENCES.md entry, [REF:rackham1940] fails validation. After applying the fixes, regenerate json/volume-2/v2.c06.l01.json with scripts/export_json.py.

l01 §4 callout: "Its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin and date from the 1st century CE — among them a short Greek epigram, and a report, passed on by Pliny the Elder, that a raven was seen dropping stones into an urn of rainwater on a tomb until the water rose within reach. Later, the Latin verse fables of Avianus (c. 400 CE) tell it as a fable, whose moral is that cleverness beats force." The callout ends "[REF:perry1952 no. 390]; [REF:rackham1940 10.125]".

Q8(b): "...its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin and date from the 1st century CE — among them a Greek epigram and Pliny's report".

New key for REFERENCES.md: rackham1940 — Pliny the Elder, Natural History, vol. III: Books 8–11, Latin text with English translation by H. Rackham, Loeb Classical Library 353, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press; London: Heinemann, 1940. Cited by book.section.

Do not add paton1917, duff1934 or piyusham5. Perry already covers the epigram and Avianus, and piyusham5 belongs to the present-day line (open item 3) with an unverified locus.

If the new key is not wanted, use this form instead and leave Pliny out: "Its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin and date from the 1st century CE; the oldest known is a short Greek epigram. Later, the Latin verse fables of Avianus (c. 400 CE) tell it as a fable, whose moral is that cleverness beats force." In that case Q8(b) becomes "...its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin and date from the 1st century CE".

claims.claim: Avianus (c. 400 CE) tells it in Latin verse, and his moral is 'that cleverness beats force'. The fable number was left open (fact base open item 4).
claims.evidence: The fable is Avianus, Fabulae 27 'De cornice et urna'. The number is confirmed by the Loeb Plutarch note ('Avianus, fable 27'), Latin Wikisource (Fabulae (Avianus)/XXVII), the Latin Library text and Laura Gibbs's Aesopica. Text: 'Ingentem sitiens cornix adspexerat urnam, / quae minimam fundo continuisset aquam …'. The crow first tries to tip the urn out over the plain; when strength (virtus) gives no way, she turns to 'nova calliditate' (new cunning); the pebbles raise the water. The closing couplet is 'Viribus haec docuit quam sit prudentia maior, / qua coeptum volucri explicuisset opus': she showed how much greater wisdom is than strength. 'Cleverness beats force' is a fair paraphrase. The bird is cornix, 'crow'. Avianus's 42 elegiac fables are dedicated to a Theodosius (possibly Macrobius) and dated c. 400 CE (Wikipedia; Sorbonne Fabula numerica). The Loeb is Duff & Duff, Minor Latin Poets (1934; vol. II = LCL 434 in the two-volume printing). Open item 4 can be closed: the number is 27.

where.section: §8 'The moral — a line written for this course'

claims.evidence: Avianus's moral is comparative: 'Viribus … quam sit prudentia maior', wisdom is greater than strength (Fabulae 27.9). The course line is an identity, 'intelligence itself is strength'. The lesson is the same (brains over brawn) but the claim is not. The Q10 key's 'it echoes Avianus's moral' is accurate; §8's 'says … what Avianus's moral says' is stronger.

II, LCL 434 in the two-volume printing (catalogue records, e.g. https://www.bokus.com/bok/9780674994782/minor-latin-poets-volume-ii); date c. 400 CE per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avianus and https://obvil.sorbonne-universite.fr/corpus/fabula-numerica/avianus_fabulae.
claims.correct_wording: The line was written for this course and quotes no text; it makes, in owned words, much the same point as Avianus's moral (§4).

challenge.reason: The problem is real, and the proposed fix is correct as written. Avianus's moral (Fabulae 27.9) is a comparison. "Viribus haec docuit quam sit prudentia maior" means she showed how much greater prudence is than strength, with viribus as an ablative of comparison. बुद्धिः एव बलम् is a verbless equation, "intelligence itself is strength", and it contains no comparison. The course's own materials record this difference. §4 says the 1.x moral "compared intelligence with strength through a case form you do not yet own". The research evidence file says it is the comparative 1.x moral बुद्धिः बलात् श्रेष्ठा whose meaning "does match Avianus's moral". It offers बुद्धिः एव बलम् only as a simpler version that uses nominatives alone. So §8's "says in owned words what Avianus's moral says" claims the two lines say the same thing, and they do not; the Q10 key's "echoes" is the accurate strength. The proposed "makes, in owned words, much the same point as Avianus's moral (§4)" is accurate and hedged, and it brings §8 into line with Q10 and §4. The quote occurs exactly once, on a single line, and the replacement keeps every house rule.

claims.claim: Pliny the Elder (1st c. CE) passes on a report of a bird 'rendered "raven" in most translations' dropping stones into an urn to raise the water (fact 0.1; l01 §27 says Pliny is not used).
claims.evidence: The core is right and the locus is right. Natural History 10.125 (Mayhoff/Loeb numbering; Bostock–Riley Book X ch. 60) reads: 'tradendum putavere memoriae quidam, visum per sitim lapides congerentem in situlam monimenti, in qua pluvia aqua durabat, sed quae attingi non posset; ita descendere paventem expressisse tali congerie quantum poturo sufficeret.' 'Certain people have thought it worth recording' shows that Pliny passes on a report and does not vouch for it. The sentence names no bird. It ends the chapter that opens 'Reddatur et corvis sua gratia' (ravens) and follows straight on from Craterus's hunting ravens (corvorum opera). The masculine participle visum fits corvus (m.), not cornix (f.), so 'raven' is the right reading. 'Most translations' cannot be counted. Rackham's Loeb (LCL 353, 1940, p. 373; seen through a search excerpt) has 'a raven was seen during a drought dropping stones into a monumental urn'. Bostock & Riley (1855) have 'A crow that was thirsty was seen heaping stones into the urn on a monument'. Holland (1601) could not be checked. Rackham, vol. III (Books 8–11), LCL 353, 1940, is confirmed. The lesson should cite the proposed key rackham1940.

claims.correct_wording: Pliny the Elder (Natural History 10.125, 1st century CE) passes on a report, 'certain people have thought it worth recording', that a raven was seen dropping stones into an urn of rainwater on a tomb until the water rose within reach. The sentence names no bird, but it closes his account of ravens (corvi); Rackham's Loeb translation has 'raven', Bostock and Riley's 'crow'. [REF:rackham1940 10.125]

challenge.reason:
The overclaim is not established, and the proposed fixes are wrong as written.

(1) The original wording has a basis on file. In /home/user/Sanskritam-Book/research/evidence/vol2-ch6-source-research.json (line 199), the chapter's own skeptic check says "Rackham's Loeb translation and Holland's both render it 'raven'; only Bostock–Riley says 'crow'". That is 2 of the 3 complete English translations, which is what "most translations" summarises. The researcher could not check Holland. Not being able to check it is not evidence against the count. Everything that can be checked also supports "raven": the Latin context, the masculine visum/poturo, and Aelian NA 2.48, which tells the same trick of Libyan κόρακες (ravens). The original already gets the two important points right: the sentence names no bird ("a bird"), and Pliny does not vouch for it ("passes on a report").

(2) The fixes would leave the lesson wrong:
(a) The l01 §27 replacement says the Pliny sentence "is used in §4's first callout". No fix adds it there. §4 (lines 131–177) mentions neither Pliny nor Rackham, so §27 would describe the lesson incorrectly.
(b) The same replacement adds [REF:rackham1940 10.125]. REFERENCES.md has no anchor for that key, and no new reference entry is proposed. validate.py checks REF keys across the whole lesson body, so this would add a validation error.
(c) "certain people have thought it worth recording" is put in quotation marks and cited to Rackham, but nobody has checked it against Rackham. Bostock–Riley reads "Some authors have thought the following circumstance deserving of remembrance". The evidence file quotes the phrase differently ("certain persons have thought it worth recording"), so at least one of the two versions is not verbatim.
(d) The notes fix's "rain-filled urn" contradicts the Latin: "in qua pluvia aqua durabat, sed quae attingi non posset" means some rainwater remained, but out of reach.
(e) "it closes his account of ravens" is imprecise. Pliny's main account of ravens is 10.32–33 (Bostock–Riley ch. 15, "The Raven"). The 10.121–125 chapter is a later set of anecdotes, and it also includes a talking cornix (crow) at 10.124.
(f) "so Rackham's Loeb has 'raven'" guesses at the translator's reasoning. "the Latin context makes a raven" says more than "the sentence names no bird" allows.

claims.decision_note: Skeptic not upheld: 'most translations' rests on the source-research record (Rackham and Holland 'raven', Bostock–Riley 'crow'); the fact base names both renderings after C03.

claims.claim: No version is known in the Pañcatantra, the Hitopadeśa or the Jātakas (brief: also any Pañcatantra recension and the Kathāsaritsāgara). The honest claim is 'no known version', never 'not Indian'.
claims.evidence: Re-checked by searching the primary e-texts themselves for any passage where a crow word (kāka, vāyasa, dhvāṅkṣa, balipuṣṭa, balibhuj, karaṭa) falls within ±300 characters of a pot word (ghaṭa, kumbha, kalaśa, kuṇḍa, karaka, bhāṇḍa, pātra) plus a stone word (pāṣāṇa, śilā, loṣṭa, śarkarā, aśman, upala) or a thirst or water word. The scan covered all 3,361 files of the GRETIL Sanskrit corpus. That includes the textus simplicior Pañcatantra (Jha ed.), both Tantrākhyāyika texts, the Hitopadeśa, Somadeva's Kathāsaritsāgara with its Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā, the Śukasaptati, the Bṛhatkathāślokasaṃgraha, the Jātakamālās of Āryaśūra, Haribhaṭṭa and Gopadatta, the Divyāvadāna, Avadānaśataka and Mahāvastu, the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas and the subhāṣita anthologies. A test sentence ('kākaḥ pipāsitaḥ ghaṭe … pāṣāṇān kṣipati') was caught, so the scan works. No real crow-and-pitcher episode turned up; the 21 residual hits were all false positives (plant names such as kākamācī, word-internal matches such as ekākinī, lists of carrion birds, a drought scene in Haribhaṭṭa's Jātakamālā). The same scan of the Pāli Jātaka verses and the whole Jātakaṭṭhakathā (VRI Chaṭṭha Saṅgāyana) also found nothing. Its nearest hit is Mahosadha seeing a jewel's reflection from a crow's nest (Mahā-ummagga), which is not this story. Not searchable here: the Sanskrit of Pūrṇabhadra's recension (Ryder 1925 not checked page by page), the southern, Nepalese and Jain Pañcatantra versions, and Kalīla wa Dimna. This is absence of attestation, so 'no known version' is exactly the right hedge and 'not Indian' is not supported. All the lesson restatements hedge correctly. claims.evidence: Perry's Aesopica (1952, Greek and Latin texts) cannot support anything about present-day India, so the citation fails. No study of Indian children's literature and no survey measuring the story's popularity was found. 'One of India's best-known' is a claim of scale with no number or source, which STYLE_GUIDE §7 rules out; it is also HISTORY-callout content without a supporting REF (§4 rule 2). Two things can be shown. (i) The Hindi title प्यासा कौआ is standard across Hindi retellings, e.g. the Kindle book 'प्यासा कौआ (The Thirsty Crow / Pyasa Kauwa)' and Grade-1 worksheets. (ii) At least one state-board Sanskrit reader retells it. The Uttar Pradesh Basic Shiksha Parishad's Class 5 reader संस्कृत पीयूषम् has a lesson 'काकस्य उद्यमः', numbered 10 in one printing and 16 in another, in which the crow, सः पिपासया आकुलः, drops पाषाण-खण्डानि into a घट. Its question key gives the moral कार्याणि उद्यमेन सिध्यन्ति, which echoes l03's Hitopadeśa verse. The plural 'Sanskrit school readers' is therefore supported for one board only. Fix: take the sentence out of the HISTORY callout. Put a plain present-day sentence after the '*No version is known*' paragraph, so that 'those books' there still points back to the Indian fable books. Cite the reader with the proposed key piyusham5 and print no superlative. If piyusham5 is not added, keep only 'in India it is told in Hindi as प्यासा कौआ' and drop the reader clause and REF.

challenge.reason:
I couldn't refute this one. STYLE_GUIDE §7 rules out "marketing superlatives" and says "Claims of scale carry numbers with sources or don't appear." All six phrases are popularity or frequency claims: 'best-known', 'favourite', 'best-loved', 'loved across India', 'almost everyone', 'the usual answer'. None of them has a number or a source anywhere in the lesson or the research files. Objective 4 also asks learners to state the history 'without overclaiming' while repeating one of these superlatives.

The one counter-argument I found is weak. Some reviewed lessons do carry unsourced fame superlatives: v1.c04.l01 'the most famous name in Sanskrit' and v2.c01.l03 'the most famous'. That shows the rule hasn't been enforced everywhere. It doesn't make these phrases comply.

The proposal is right overall but needs three small corrections:
- **Fixes 7 and 8** say 'told/retold in India today as प्यासा कौआ'. That ties a Hindi title to all of India, which is the same overgeneralisation fix 3 removes when it replaces 'across India it is told as प्यासा कौआ' with 'in Hindi'. It also contradicts the proposal's own rule ('in Hindi the story is प्यासा कौआ'). The l05 homework is also done 'in any language'. Both should say 'in Hindi'.
- **Fix 3** keeps 'long before they can read'. The cited sources don't show this: one is a Grade-1 worksheet for children who already read and write, the other a children's ebook. The proposal's own wording only says 'told to small children', so the fix should trim to that.

Everything else holds:
- Each quote occurs exactly once in its file.
- The patched files pass the validator with no errors.
- No quiz item tests the dropped clause, so no quiz change is needed.

claims.claim: l05 §1: 'You also know where those stories come from, which is more than the 1.x book knew.'
claims.evidence: The chapter teaches where the stories are first found or attested and explicitly refuses origin claims: l01 §4 ('not proof of where it began'), l02 §4 ('no claim about which came first'), l05 §22 ('absence of attestation, nothing more'). 'Know where those stories come from' claims the origin knowledge the course disowns. The 1.x book printed the crow as 'तृष्णार्तः काकः — A famous fable' and made no origin claim at all (PDF p. 64).

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. In l05 itself, "come from" means origin. The Station 1 key, §12 row 1, the task D card 5 key and §22 all reject "it does not come from India" as an origin claim, because the evidence "says nothing about origin" and "supports absence of attestation, nothing more". l01 §4 says the evidence shows where the crow story "is first written down, not where it was first told". So the hook's unhedged "you know where those stories come from" claims knowledge the chapter says nobody has, in the very lesson that marks learners down for unhedged origin claims.

The second half, "more than the 1.x book knew", is a claim about what the 1.x book knew, and nobody can check that. The PDF only printed no source for either story.

The proposed fix needs one change. "First found" works for the crow, but not for the lion. l02 never names an earliest version of the lion story: it gives an Aesopic telling (no date), a Demotic one (2nd c. CE) and Indian cousins, and it refuses to rank them. Dropping "first" makes the line accurate for both stories.

The Station 1 key drops the scope of its claim: "The evidence shows that no version is attested" is false as written, and it contradicts the first clause of the same answer ("its earliest known versions are Greek and Latin"). The primary texts confirm a Greek version (Bianor, Greek Anthology 9.272) and Latin ones (Pliny, Natural History 10.125; Avianus 27). Restricting the claim to India doesn't save it either. l01 §4 itself reports modern Hindi and Sanskrit school-reader tellings. The replacement breaks no house rule, and the edited file passes the project validator. No change to the proposal is needed.

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The sentence in l05 §7, प्रमाण केवल इतना बताता है कि कोई भारतीय रूप दर्ज नहीं है ("the evidence only shows that no Indian version is recorded"), is wrong as worded and claims too much.

1. **It is false if read literally, and the course contradicts it.** l01 §4's HISTORY callout says the story is "one of India's best-known children's stories — in Hindi, प्यासा कौआ — and Sanskrit school readers tell it too". The l01 §1 hook and the l05 §26 reel script ("India made it one of its best-loved children's stories") say the same.
2. **It breaks the chapter's own wording rule.** Research note 0.1 says: Say "no known version", never "no Indian text contains it". The sentence is close to the banned phrase. It also drops "known" (ज्ञात) and the named books, turning a statement about the evidence into a flat statement about the world. The skeptic check in the evidence file flags exactly this kind of blanket negative as under-hedged.
3. **A flat denial invites an easy challenge.** Archaeologist B.B. Lal read a painted Lothal vase as the thirsty-crow scene. That reading is contested, but Indian competitive-exam guides give it as a stock answer. The research file warns that "a flat denial invites challenge".

The context, which names the Pañcatantra, Hitopadeśa and Jātakas just before, does not save the sentence. It is the one line where the paragraph preaching "जितना पक्का है उतना कहना, उससे ज़्यादा नहीं" (say only as much as is certain) says more than the evidence supports.

**The proposed wording is accurate and hedged.** पुराने भारतीय कथा-ग्रन्थों में इसका कोई रूप दर्ज नहीं मिलता ("no version of it is found recorded in the old Indian story-books"):
- It is limited to old written texts, so it stays true despite modern retellings and the Lothal vase, which is not a book.
- "नहीं मिलता" (is not found) reports what searches found, not that no version exists. That matches the course's "no known version".
- It matches what the chapter already says in English: l05 §12 row 1 ("in the Indian fable books"), l01 §12 and l02 §4 ("India's old fable books at all").
- कथा-ग्रन्थ follows the course's Hindi usage (ग्रन्थ spelling; l02 §7 has "भारत की कथा-पुस्तकों").

**House rules and mechanics:**
- The new text has no parentheses, IPA, references, quotation marks, dates or time-depth figures, and it sits in §7 prose, not a callout.
- The quote occurs exactly once in the lesson file.
- On a scratch copy with the fix applied, `validate.py` reports 0 errors and 0 warnings.
- The same sentence is in the generated file json/volume-2/v2.c06.l05.json. CI runs `export_json.py --check`, so the JSON must be re-exported after the edit, not edited by hand.

topics.notes:
Method and limits. The fact base, the source-research JSON, all five lessons, chapter.md, REFERENCES.md and the two house-rule files were read in full, and the 1.x PDF p. 64 was extracted with pdftotext. Primary texts were read from GitHub mirrors: Perseus canonical-latinLit for Pliny NH 10.121–125 (Mayhoff's Latin and Bostock–Riley 1855); Perseus canonical-greekLit for AP 9.272 (Paton vol. III), Plutarch De sollertia animalium (Bernardakis, and Cherniss–Helmbold's Loeb) and Aelian NA 2.48 (Hercher); the Latin Library mirror for Avianus 27; Cologne csl-orig for MW and Apte. The absence check (C07) scanned the GRETIL Sanskrit corpus and the VRI Pāli Tipiṭaka. WebFetch could not reach non-GitHub hosts, so other web pages were seen only through search results. The session's web-search budget ran out at the very end, so the LCL serial number of Paton vol. III was not confirmed and is left out of the proposed paton1917 entry.

Simulation. All 24 fixes and the four proposed REFERENCES entries were applied to scratch copies: every quote matched exactly once at the moment it was applied, and scripts/validate.py reports 0 errors and 0 warnings for chapter 6. No repo file was edited. Two fix pairs share a passage without overlapping: C03 and C10 in the l01 callout, and C06 and C10 in l01 §27. In the l01 callout, C03 (first half) and C10 (second half) must both be applied, or neither. If the editors decline the new keys, use the minimal C03 wording given in its correct_wording and drop the reader clause from C10.

Open items. Item 1 (Pliny) is resolved by C03 and C06 with rackham1940. Item 3 (the present-day sentence) is resolved by C10 and C11. Item 4: the Avianus fable number is 27, so l01 §27's 'no fable number given' flag can be updated.

(e) Scientific aside. None exists in l01–l05 or chapter.md: grep for experiment, rook, jay, Caledonian, Emery, Jelbert, corvid, raven and Pliny found nothing outside l01 §27's Pliny flag. If one is added, these are verified:
- Bird & Emery 2009, 'Rooks use stones to raise the water level to reach a floating worm', Current Biology 19(16): 1410–1414, doi:10.1016/j.cub.2009.07.033. Four captive rooks; they used about the number of stones needed and came to prefer larger stones. Rooks are not known to use tools in the wild.
- Jelbert, Taylor, Cheke, Clayton & Gray 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3): e92895, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0092895. New Caledonian crows preferred water- over sand-filled tubes, sinking over floating and solid over hollow objects, and the higher water level. They failed a tube-width task and a U-tube task. The authors call their understanding of displacement 'sophisticated but incomplete'.
- Ghirlanda & Lind 2017, Animal Behaviour 123: 239–247. Reanalysing 33 such experiments, they found the results consistent with trial-and-error learning and little evidence of causal understanding.
Any aside must be a hedged FACT callout with new keys (e.g. bird2009, jelbert2014, ghirlanda2017), and should not repeat press comparisons to 5–7-year-old children.

Note on the bird. The ancient natural-history witnesses (Pliny, Plutarch's κόρακες, Aelian's Λίβυες κόρακες) all mean ravens, and Bianor's bird is just 'Phoebus' servant'. Only Avianus has cornix 'crow'. The modern fable and the lesson's काकः say 'crow'; the course need not change anything, but should not say the Greek or Pliny says 'crow'.

Other findings.
- Plutarch (De soll. an. 10, 967A) says he once took the Libyan-raven tale for a myth until he saw a ship's dog drop pebbles into a half-empty oil jar. Aelian (NA 2.48) has Libyan ravens dropping pebbles into rooftop jars, 'knowing that two bodies do not occupy one place'. Both are optional background; neither is needed in the lesson.
- The pseudo-Dositheus (2nd–3rd c.) version is reported only by Wikipedia; keep it out.
- The Lothal-jar reading appears in no lesson, as fact 0.1 requires.
- The source-research JSON's remark that Apte also gives śreṣṭha with the ablative is wrong: Apte has only gen./loc. Fact 0.3 rightly cites MW only, and Manusmṛti 12.103 is a clean classical example.
- The UP reader's moral, कार्याणि उद्यमेन सिध्यन्ति, echoes l03's Hitopadeśa verse. That could be a Teacher Note link, but the wording was seen only in third-party answer keys.

Outside this topic but noticed. l05 rung 5's 'under 40 seconds' conflicts with l01's natural pace (≈65 s) and timed bar (<50 s) (open item 5; Pass D). chapter.md's 'the Indian cousin of the lion story' is singular, against l02's two cousins (lion researcher).

topics.topic: The Lion and the Mouse — history, cousins and the 1.x text (v2.c06: lesson 2, chapter.md, exam, fact base §0.2/§0.4)

claims.claim: 'The Lion and the Mouse' is Aesopic fable no. 150 in Perry's index (brief a: confirm the number; earliest Greek/Latin witnesses).
claims.evidence: Perry 150 = 'The Lion and the Mouse' is consistent across Wikipedia (Perry Index 150), Wikidata (Perry 150 = Babrius 107 = Halm 256) and L. Gibbs's Aesopica page perry/150 titled THE LION AND THE MOUSE (one Wikipedia list-mirror shifts it to 151, an isolated mis-row). Earliest witnesses: the oldest securely datable Greek telling is Babrius, fable 107 (choliambic verse; Babrius fl. 1st-2nd c. CE, date debated: Britannica 'fl. 2nd century AD'); Perry's no. 150 text itself is the prose Augustana version, whose date is uncertain. I found no Phaedrus version (nothing ties this fable to Phaedrus); in Latin it appears in the medieval Romulus prose tradition ('Leo et mus' among the Romulus vulgaris titles). The earliest Greek witness (Babrius) and the Demotic papyrus (2nd c. CE) are thus roughly contemporary, which is one more reason the course's 'no claim about which came first' is the right posture. The lessons name no Babrius/Phaedrus locus, so nothing needs changing; if a witness is ever added, say 'Babrius (fable 107)' and do not name Phaedrus.

claims.claim: The same tale is told inside an Egyptian narrative written in Demotic in the 2nd century CE, the 'Myth of the Sun's Eye' (brief b: papyrus, date).
claims.evidence: The Demotic 'Myth of the Sun's Eye' is preserved on Papyrus Leiden I 384 (recto), ed. Spiegelberg 1917 ('nach dem Leidener demotischen Papyrus I 384'); Trismegistos/DCLP TM 55946 dates the roll AD 100-199, written at Dios Polis (Thebes); the TLA labels the columns 'Roman period'; the verso carries later Greek and Demotic magic (PGM XII / PDM xii). The fable embedded in it - a lion spares a small mouse that begs for its life; later, caught by a hunter, the lion is bound and the mouse frees him - occupies papyrus cols. 17/9-18/34 (Lichtheim's introduction, as reproduced in a Charles University course file), and Lichtheim notes that this final episode 'also occurs in a shorter version among the Fables of Aesop'. A Greek translation of the Myth survives on a 3rd-century papyrus (British Museum 274). '2nd century CE' is the date of the Leiden copy (palaeographic range); the composition date of the narrative is not established and may be earlier - the lessons' Q10 key already treats it as a 'date of writing', so the wording is accurate. Optional precision for the two main callouts: 'preserved in a Demotic papyrus of the 2nd century CE'.

claims.claim: In the Egyptian (Demotic) telling, as in the Aesopic, the mouse frees the lion 'by gnawing through ropes'.
claims.evidence: 'Ropes' fits the Greek tellings (Babrius/Augustana: lion caught by hunters, bound or netted, mouse gnaws the cords) but not the Demotic one. In Lichtheim's translation (as reproduced by attalus.org and the Iseum Sanctuary retelling, both after AEL III pp. 157-159) a hunter's pit and net catch the lion, he is bound with dry and with raw leather straps (thongs/fetters), and the little mouse cuts the dry straps and gnaws through the raw ones. Since the parenthesis describes 'the same tale' in both traditions, the neutral 'his bonds' is exact for both.

claims.correct_wording: The same tale — a lion spares a mouse, and the mouse later frees him by gnawing through his bonds — is also told inside an Egyptian narrative ...

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The problem is real and the fix is right.

The parenthesis gives one description of "the same tale", with ropes in it, and then says that tale "is also told" in the Demotic narrative. So it credits the Egyptian telling with ropes. In Lichtheim's translation of "The Lion in Search of Man" (the episode of the Myth of the Sun's Eye, Leiden Demotic Papyrus I 384), there are no ropes. The lion falls into a hunter's pit and is put in a net. He is bound with dry straps and tied with raw ones. The mouse sets his mouth to the lion's fetters, cuts the dry straps and gnaws through the raw ones. German translations agree (trockene and frische Riemen, i.e. leather thongs). Ropes do fit the Greek: in the Augustana Aesop the hunters tie the lion to a tree with a rope (σχοινίον), and in Babrius the lion is in hunters' nets.

The course holds itself to this level of detail elsewhere. It teaches "ropes, not nets" for the Pañcatantra elephants, so a wrong binding material for Egypt fails its own standard.

"His bonds" is accurate for every telling: rope, net cords, leather straps and fetters are all bonds. It also matches बद्धः in the course's own retelling. The fix is safe even if some translation says "cords".

The repo's earlier evidence ("the mouse bites through the rope", vol2-ch6-source-research.json item 2b) is a paraphrase taken from a search snippet. The lesson's own §27 Pass C flag says the [REF:lichtheim1980] citation still has to be checked against the book.

This is not an overclaim. The clause denies a lion-and-mouse *version*, meaning a telling of this tale in which a lion spares a mouse and the mouse later frees him. It does not deny that any story with a lion and a mouse exists. The researcher's own evidence concedes the clause is "true for this tale". The Hitopadeśa Book 2 story of the lion, the mouse and the cat Dadhikarṇa has an unrelated plot and moral, so it is not a version and does not falsify the clause.

But the course itself counts the Pañcatantra cousin as a version: v2.c06.l05 Q6 asks "what does the course claim about which version came first?" All three fix quotes occur exactly once, and the replacements break no formatting rule, but the change is not warranted. The problem is still real, in a lesson whose stated aim is history told "without overclaiming in either direction".

The proposed wording is accurate and needs no recension hedge, because the pigeon frame is in the textus simplicior, which the `panchatantra` key uses by default. It has two flaws, fixed below:

(2) It adds a new claim about where the episode sits in the Pañcatantra with no citation. Both keys needed (`panchatantra`, `hitopadesha`) already exist in REFERENCES.md.

claims.claim: अहिंसा परमो धर्मः occurs in the BORI critical edition at 1.11.12, 3.198.69, 13.116.1, 13.116.25 and 13.117.37 (the five loci, their wording and speakers).
claims.evidence: Searched the BORI critical-edition e-text (GRETIL mbh_01–18_u.htm, which also carries every star (*) and appendix (@) passage) with sandhi-tolerant patterns, then re-checked verse by verse. The main (constituted) text has exactly five hits, with this wording: (1) 1.11.12ab ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ sarvaprāṇabhṛtāṃ smṛtaḥ | 12cd tasmāt prāṇabhṛtaḥ sarvān na hiṃsyād brāhmaṇaḥ kva cit. Speaker: the sage Sahasrapād (1.10.7), who had been turned into a harmless ḍuṇḍubha snake and has regained his own form (1.11.11c svarūpaṃ pratilabhya); he speaks to Ruru. (2) 3.198.69, a six-pāda verse, with the phrase in pāda c: ahiṃsā satyavacanaṃ sarvabhūtahitaṃ param | ahiṃsā paramo dharmaḥ sa ca satye pratiṣṭhitaḥ | satye kṛtvā pratiṣṭhāṃ tu pravartante pravṛttayaḥ. Speaker: the hunter (vyādha uvāca, 3.198.57) teaching the brahmin, inside Mārkaṇḍeya's narration. (3) 13.116.1ab, spoken by Yudhiṣṭhira: ahiṃsā paramo dharma ity uktaṃ bahuśas tvayā | cd śrāddheṣu ca bhavān āha pitṝn āmiṣakāṅkṣiṇaḥ. (4) 13.116.25, spoken by Bhīṣma (bhīṣma uvāca at 13.116.7): ahiṃsā paramo dharmas tathāhiṃsā paraṃ tapaḥ | ahiṃsā paramaṃ satyaṃ tato dharmaḥ pravartate. (5) 13.117.37, spoken by Bhīṣma (13.117.6): ahiṃsā paramo dharmas tathāhiṃsā paro damaḥ | ahiṃsā paramaṃ dānam ahiṃsā paramaṃ tapaḥ. The chain continues at 13.117.38: ahiṃsā paramo yajñas … paramaṃ śrutam. At three of the five loci the last word shows sandhi (dharma ity; dharmas tathā). No pāda-split, inflected or word-order variant exists elsewhere in the main text. One disagreement to note: Bandyopadhyay (Seminar 608, 2010; Global-e 2018) reports Hiltebeitel's (2001) count as 'ahiṃsā paramo dharma' four times among 54 'paramo dharma(ḥ)' (ānṛśaṃsya eight times). I could not see Hiltebeitel's list. The CE e-text plainly gives five main-text lines, so the course's five stands; the gap is probably a counting choice, for example whether Yudhiṣṭhira's quotation at 13.116.1 counts.

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The facts hold and the underlying problem is real, but the proposed fixes need some changes. I searched the GRETIL copy of the BORI critical-edition (CE) e-text myself. The phrase occurs exactly five times in the main text and three more times in passages the edition rejected, at the loci the researcher gives. The strongest counter-argument is convention. Scholars use "in the critical edition" to mean the constituted text, and the lesson's own §4 callout describes the CE as printing "the text they support". On that reading the original wording is ordinary shorthand. That defence fails for this audience. The hook tells learners to "Open the Mahābhārata's critical edition and you will find it five times". The standard e-text interleaves the star and appendix lines, so a learner who checks finds eight hits. The lesson's own Pass C flags (§27) also treat "the critical-edition e-text, including star and appendix passages" as one body of text. So "main text" is a needed precision fix, more an imprecision than an overclaim.

The proposal is factually right. All nine quotes occur exactly once, and applying them leaves validate.py clean. I am upholding it with these changes:
(1) It leaves four statements that still assume five places in total. The worst is the misquotation callout's "At none of the five places where अहिंसा परमो धर्मः occurs", which comes about 20 lines after the new "three more times" sentence and contradicts it. The others are the model reply "at all five places", the voice-over at 01:50 ("At all five places in the critical edition"), which is heard without any callout, and the l05 Station 3 key "the line's five places".
(2) "three times more" can be read as multiplying, so it becomes "three more times".
(3) The Hindi fix stacks two locatives ("संस्करण में … उसके मुख्य पाठ में"); "यह पंक्ति मुख्य पाठ में पाँच बार आती है" reads better.
(4) Star passages are printed in the footnotes (the critical apparatus), so "footnotes" is more exact than "notes".
(5) The research note should say that the count of three comes from an e-text that does not carry the variant readings.

The added line धर्महिंसा तथैव च is at none of these eight places.

claims.claim: 'धर्महिंसा तथैव च' is not in the Mahābhārata as critically edited. At none of the five loci does the verse continue this way, and no source for the line has been found.
claims.evidence: Zero hits in the CE e-text for dharma(-)hiṃsā, 'hiṃsā tathaiva ca' or 'dharmahiṃs', in Unicode IAST including ṁ/ṃ variants and Devanagari forms. The search covered the main text and every star and appendix passage. The real continuations: 1.11.12b sarvaprāṇabhṛtāṃ smṛtaḥ; 3.198.69d sa ca satye pratiṣṭhitaḥ; 13.116.1b ity uktaṃ bahuśas tvayā; 13.116.25b tathāhiṃsā paraṃ tapaḥ; 13.117.37b tathāhiṃsā paro damaḥ. I could not refute the finding. "Not in the critical edition anywhere" (§20) and "समीक्षित संस्करण में यह जोड़ कहीं नहीं है" (§7) say the line is absent from every part of the edition. The cited [REF:mahabharata] is the 19-volume printed BORI edition, which includes the variant apparatus. The check behind the claim covered only the e-text: the constituted text plus the star and Appendix I passages. The course's own dossier names the apparatus as unchecked and recommends the narrower wording "not in the Mahābhārata as critically edited", which §8 already uses. §7 also commits to giving each source "उतनी ही पक्की बात के साथ … जितना सचमुच पता है", so an unchecked "कहीं नहीं" breaks the lesson's own standard.

The strongest counter-argument is that the course uses "critical edition" to mean the constituted text: its "five times" count leaves out the three star and appendix hits. That does not rescue "anywhere", because "anywhere" explicitly widens the scope beyond the text.

The English fix is correct as proposed. The Hindi fix is accurate but needs one change. It uses पाठ to mean "text", but GLOSSARY.md defines पाठ as "lesson", and two sentences later the same paragraph says "इसलिए यह पाठ उसे … दिखाता है", meaning "this lesson". With the fix, a reader could take that "यह पाठ" to mean the critical edition's text, which would wrongly say the edition labels the line a misquotation. I reworded it to avoid पाठ, keep the paragraph's term समीक्षित संस्करण, and match §8's scope.

claims.evidence: The अ is elided (Whitney §135). ऽ is a written sign that marks where it was (§16a); the vowel does not turn into it. l02 §7 says this correctly: 'जहाँ वह था, वहाँ अवग्रह ऽ लिखा जाता है'. So do l03 §3 key 1 and §8 ('marked by the avagraha').

challenge.reason: I could not refute the finding. The Hindi line says the अ "लुप्त होकर ऽ बन गया" (disappeared and became ऽ), which contradicts itself and treats a sound as if it turned into a written sign. §13's "disappeared into ऽ" says the same thing as a metaphor. Whitney gives a different account. The a "disappears" (§135) or "is lost" (§175a), and it is "absorbed into the preceding diphthong" (§135a, c), which means into the ओ, not into ऽ. The avagraha is a "separator" sign that printed texts ordinarily use "to mark the elision" (§16a). The course describes it the same way everywhere else: the GLOSSARY ("marks a dropped अ"), l02 §7/§12/§15/§19 Q5, l03's own §3 key 1, §15 FACT and §18 Exercise 2 key, and the l05 exam key for item 7, which assesses exactly this description ("disappears, marked by the avagraha ऽ"). These two lines are the only places in the chapter that say otherwise. Both fixes are accurate, each quote occurs exactly once, and the replacements keep the house rules. One small caveat about the general wording: by Whitney §16a, writing ऽ is the ordinary convention of printed texts, while manuscripts use it only occasionally. Both fixes describe the printed word कोऽपि, where ऽ is in fact written, so they need no hedge.

In the Hitopadeśa's introduction, verse 36 (udyamena hi sidhyanti…) is not the end of King Sudarśana's reflection, and he does not convene the paṇḍitas straight after it. Three more verses of the reflection come first, on the disgrace of lacking learning, starting with 'mātā śatruḥ pitā vairī yena bālo na pāṭhitaḥ'. Only then does the narrative close the reflection with 'etac cintayitvā rājā paṇḍita-sabhāṃ kāritavān'. So the lesson's 'This verse ends his reflection. He then calls the learned together' is wrong. Even read narrowly, 'He then' skips three verses. The proposed replacement is accurate. '0.36 closes the fate-against-effort weighing' is right: the fate verses are 0.27–0.29 and the effort verses 0.30–0.36. 'A few more verses' is suitably hedged: there are 3 in GRETIL and DCS, and Apte's numbering implies 4. 'On why a child must be taught' is a fair summary of 0.37–0.39 and is not in quotation marks. The fix quote occurs exactly once, and the replacement breaks no house rule. No adjustment is needed.

claims.claim: मनोरथ = मनस् + रथ, 'literally "chariot of the mind"' = 'a wish' (l03 table, note, Hindi §7, Q6; fact base 0.7).
claims.evidence: Every source agrees on the analysis मनस् + रथ, with -as → -o before a voiced sound (Whitney §175a, whose examples include manobhava), and on the meaning 'wish'. They disagree on what this रथ means. Apte s.v. मनस्: '-रथः 1 "the car of the mind", a wish, desire'. Monier-Williams 1899 p. 785 s.v. mano-ratha: 'm. "heart's joy" (see 2. ratha), a wish, desire (also = desired object), MBh.; Kāv.', where 2. ratha (p. 866) is 'm. (√ram) pleasure, joy, delight (cf. mano-ratha)'. MW gives 'the heart compared to a car (see 1. ratha), R.' only as a separate Rāmāyaṇa sense. The MW Additions (p. 1331) add: 'accord. to some orig. Prākṛt for mano'rtha, "heart-matter"'. Böhtlingk–Roth, vol. 5 col. 533: '(manas + ratha, nom. act. von ram; vgl. manorama) … Wunsch (Herzensfreude)', quoting this very verse. Their Nachträge (vol. 7 col. 1787) allow 'der Wagen Herz, das als Wagen gedachte Herz' only for the pun at R. 5.21.6 (saṃkalpa-haya-saṃyuktair yāntīm iva manorathaiḥ). So 'literally "chariot of the mind"' presents Apte's explanation as the settled literal meaning, which MW and PWG contradict. The brief's request to 'confirm MW' fails: MW does not support 'chariot of the mind'. Hindi does use मनोरथ for 'wish', as the lesson says. The key to Q6 ('मनस् + रथ, learned whole') is fine.

claims.claim: The printed verse उद्यमेन… has no joins between words, so the pause form equals the joined original; some editions print न हि as नहि; मनोरथैः is one word.
claims.evidence: I checked every word boundary: udyamena | hi | sidhyanti | kāryāṇi | na | manorathaiḥ ‖ na | hi | suptasya | siṃhasya | praviśanti | mukhe | mṛgāḥ. Each first word ends in a vowel before a consonant, and no rule changes either sound. The visarga of manorathaiḥ stands at the end of the half-verse, which printed texts treat as a pause, so no -ir sandhi applies. The differences between texts are orthographic only: नहि as one word (GRETIL Hit_0.36, MSS 6888) and anusvāra spellings such as सिध्यंति (Apte's printing). The join inside मनोरथ is word-internal, as the lessons say.

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the main point. 'Two-word essence' is wrong as a description of the couplet, and it contradicts the lesson's own reading of it. The verse's phrase is वचनद्वयम्, which l03 glosses 'a pair of sayings' (line 433) and translates 'Vyāsa's two sayings' (line 405). §7 has 'व्यास के दो वचन'. What the verse delivers is two sayings of two words each, four words in all: परोपकारः पुण्याय · पापाय परपीडनम्.

The only defence I could build was that 'word' can mean 'utterance': Apte gives वचनम् as 'words (spoken)', so 'two-word' could be read as a loose calque of वचन-द्वयम्. It fails. Used before a noun, 'two-word' counts dictionary words, and the course itself always uses it that way, in English and in Hindi. So 'two-word' and 'दो-शब्दों वाला' read as a count of words, and Q8's keyed answer states that count.

The Hook part of the claim is the weaker half. §4 ('traditionally Vyāsa's teaching in two phrases') and §25 ('the essence of Vyāsa's teaching') say 'Vyāsa's teaching' with no scope either, and the researcher leaves both alone. Still, the verse's own scope is अष्टादशपुराणेषु, 'in the eighteen Purāṇas'. The new Hook wording ('the whole of Vyāsa's eighteen Purāṇas in two phrases') matches that and does no harm.

The proposal holds up:
- Its wording is accurate to the verse and stays hedged ('traditionally quoted as …').
- Sternbach MSS no. 3587 (the couplet) and Apte (the glosses) support it.
- Every fix keeps the house rules: no new parenthesis after a Devanagari word, no new REF keys, TRADITION stays attributed, and Q8 still opens 'According to the tradition'.

Small blemishes, none an error:
- Fix 2 drops the comma the other versions have ('Purāṇas summed up').
- The Hindi objective does not carry the eighteen-Purāṇas scope that the English objective now has.
- Fixes 11–13 use shorter versions of the wording.
- Several replacement lines run past the usual ~90-column wrap. The validator has no line-length rule.

challenge.reason:
This is not a real overclaim, and the fixes only swap in near-synonyms.

1. The one alternative frame I could verify does not make "usually" false. The Pañcatantra (textus simplicior, Jha ed.) 3.103 does give the line another first line. But "usually" does not mean "always". Apte quotes the line alone, which is ordinary dictionary practice for a half-line and says nothing about which first line it circulates with.
2. The researcher agrees that the Vyāsa couplet is the best-known form today. The lesson's "it usually travels with" is in the present tense, so it already describes current circulation. That is what "today it is most often quoted with" says. "Usually" and "most often" mean much the same, and so do "usual" and "popular". The new wording rests on the same evidence as the old (MSS 3587 plus modern web pages), so it is no better sourced.
3. The finding contradicts itself. It accepts the Hindi of §7, "परम्परा इसे प्रायः … सुनाती है" (prāyaḥ means "usually, mostly"), and the Hindi objective's "प्रचलित". Those make the same claim as the English "usually". The fix set also leaves l03 §7, the l05 §4 callout ("usually after") and the l05 Q8 key ("The line usually quoted") as they are, unless separate fixes (C13, C14) land; I could not confirm those. Applied alone, these fixes would make the chapter's wording inconsistent.
4. The proposed wording has its own problems:
   - "वचनद्वयम् (its popular first line)" puts English inside a parenthesis directly after a Devanagari word. That breaks the house rule that such a parenthesis holds only that word's IAST.
   - "Other texts give it other first lines, among them the Pañcatantra" says "texts" in the plural, but only one text is verified. The Vikramacarita and ślokārdhena frames rest on search snippets (the researcher says the recension was not checked). "Vyāsena kathitaṃ dvayam" is just a variant of the same Vyāsa line.
   - The only new piece of information, the Pañcatantra frame, is not in any of the four fixes.

All four fix quotes do occur exactly once, and the replacement texts follow the house rules. That does not save a finding whose problem is not real.

A separate, optional improvement for the editors: the course's own source research (item 3a) recommended mentioning the Pañcatantra 3.103 frame with [REF:panchatantra tantra 3]. That would add information; it is not a fix for an overclaim.

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. Calling the line "later" is a relative date. No source in the course supports it, and the line's own form does not imply it. Purāṇas themselves name "the eighteen Purāṇas" and speak of Vyāsa in the third person, so a summary of that shape does not have to come after the Purāṇas. The date sits uncited inside a TRADITION callout (exam §4), which breaks EDITORIAL §2.1: a HISTORY claim with no citation must be softened or deleted. The Q8 key then tests it, which STYLE_GUIDE §4 rule 4 forbids for HISTORY that is not taught in a cited HISTORY callout. The exam reviews l03, and l03 never taught "later": it says only "a summary that credits the thought to Vyāsa", and its teacher notes say "no dates anywhere in the lesson". Research evidence 3a does not say "later" either; the word first appears in fact base 0.8, with no source.

The proposal is right in substance: drop "later" and describe the line as a summary that credits Vyāsa and speaks of him from outside. Its fixes need three changes. (1) It fixes only the Q8 key. Exam §4, the callout the key cites, and fact base 0.8 would still say "later summary", even though the claim names both. (2) The Q8 replacement also rewrites "traditionally quoted as the two-word essence of his teaching" and changes "usually" to "most often". Both changes are outside this finding, and the key would then disagree with §4 and with the wording of the Q8 question. (3) "Its date and origin are unknown" claims a little more than was checked, because Sternbach's source list for no. 3587 was not seen. What the evidence supports is "no dated attestation has been found". The lessons need no date clause at all.
challenge.better_wording: That first line is not traced to any Purāṇa; it is a summary that credits the thought to Vyāsa (it speaks of him from outside). Lessons and keys need no date clause, matching l03's "no dates" policy. The fact base adds a drafting note instead: no dated attestation of that line has been found, so do not call it "later" or give it a date.

challenge.reason:
The problem is real, but the fixes as submitted cannot be applied.

THE PROBLEM IS REAL
- Apte 1890 s.v. पर (-उपकारः) gives only the line परोपकारः पुण्याय पापाय परपीडनं. It has no first line, no Vyāsa frame and no locus.
- l05 §4 still hangs four claims on that one REF: "in the subhāṣita collections", the Vyāsa framing, "usually after the line…" and "not traced".
- l03 §8 quotes the full couplet with no locus, although one exists (MSS 3587). The lesson's own Pass C flag (4) shows why Sternbach was left out: "not cited (no key)". That is a gap in the process, not a choice about content. The chapter's evidence file had already recommended both [REF:sternbach1974 3587] and the Pañcatantra parallel.
- The second line's only premodern literary attestation is not mentioned. It is Pañcatantra (Jha ed.) 3.103, under a different first line, in the cat Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra's sermon; the cat then eats both animals. This attestation supports the lesson's own "not traced / a summary" point.
- The Kathāsaritsāgara cat story (10.6.47–55) lacks the line. Corpus searches find the line only in MSS 3587 and Pañc. 3.103.
- l04's Station 0 key needs no change. Its REF only has to support the line's currency, and its wording matches l03.

WHY THE PROPOSAL NEEDS CORRECTION
1. Dangling key. Two lessons would cite [REF:sternbach1974 3587], but no fix adds that anchor. On a scratch copy, validate.py reports 2 errors: "[REF:sternbach1974] does not resolve".
2. The l05 rewrite goes beyond the finding:
   - "two-word essence" becomes "…summed up in two sayings";
   - "usually" becomes "most often";
   - "later summary" becomes "an anthology verse, a summary".
   This breaks l05's own key 8(b) ("two-word essence…; it is a later summary (§4; l03 §8)") and its match with l03 and l04. If "two-word essence" is to change, it must change across the whole chapter in one pass.
3. The research-note rewrite adds two unverified claims: "other first lines also circulate" (the corpora show only two first lines, MSS 3587's and Pañc. 3.103's) and "today most often".
4. The REFERENCES text "cited tantra.verse (e.g. 3.103)" contradicts the same entry's "cited by tantra and story". It also contradicts the chapter's rule against Pañcatantra verse numbers in lessons (l03 §22, notes 0.7), and numbering differs by edition (Apte "Pt. 2.131" against Jha 2.136).
5. One piece of evidence proves nothing. "Not in the Tantrākhyāyika e-texts" says nothing about Book III: GRETIL's Tantrākhyāyika files hold only Books I and II, and the cat story is in Book III. Naming a Sanskrit textus-simplicior edition is still justified on other grounds.
6. After the fix, l03's Pass C flag ("Sternbach's anthology is not cited (no key)") would be false.

UNVERIFIED, SO KEPT OUT OF THE FIXES
- The MSS vol. II details (1976; nos. 1874–4208; VIS 69).
- Hertel's and Penzer's dating.
- Pūrṇabhadra's Sanskrit text.

The corrected fixes below keep the original wording and only add the locus and the parallel, each with its REF. On a scratch copy they validate: 61 lessons, 0 errors.

claims.claim: 'Not traced' means that no one has located it.
claims.evidence: The course can say that no source has been found in the texts searched; it cannot know that 'no one' anywhere has located one. The rest of the sentence (a different claim from 'proven absent') is right, and l03's misquotation callout already uses the correct form, 'no source … has been found'.
sources: See C15 (search coverage and limits)
claims.correct_wording: "Not traced" means that no source has been found for it, which is a different claim from "proven absent".

challenge.reason: I could not refute the finding. The sentence at l03 line 423 defines "not traced" as "no one has located it". That turns a report on a limited search into a claim about everyone's knowledge. The course's own research does not support that claim: it says plainly that whole Purāṇas went unsearched and that the source list for the one entry that does record the couplet was never seen. The lesson promises source lines "as firm as the evidence and no firmer", so the definition is a real overclaim, though a small one. The proposed wording, "no source has been found for it", is the formula the house already uses for the same kind of negative result: the misquotation callout, Teacher Notes, the voice-over and Pass C flag (2) all use it. It keeps the contrast with "proven absent" and still parallels v1.c06.l04's "source unrecorded". It is also accurate if "source" is read broadly, because no text that could be the first line's origin turns up in any searched corpus. One caveat: the agentless passive is close in logic to "no one has located it". Its advantage is that it does not claim to know what everyone else has searched. Adding "so far" would be acceptable but is not needed. The fix quote occurs exactly once, and the replacement is plain English with no Devanagari, IPA, REF key, callout, "descend" or dates, so it breaks no house rule. No Hindi line needs a matching change. json/volume-2/v2.c06.l03.json is generated from the markdown by scripts/export_json.py, so it does not need its own fix.

claims.claim: व्यासस्य 'of Vyāsa' shows that the line speaks about Vyāsa from outside; it is a summary crediting him (l03 §8, §7, Q9, §25).
claims.evidence: व्यासस्य is a genitive singular in the third person, so the line describes Vyāsa's sayings rather than voicing them. That the couplet sums up 'the eighteen Purāṇas' as 'two sayings of Vyāsa' is what it literally says. A third-person reference alone would not prove a non-Purāṇic origin, since Purāṇic narrators also speak of Vyāsa in the third person, but the lessons do not claim it does. Q9's distractor (c) is rightly wrong: the genitive tells you nothing about a Purāṇic locus.
sources: W.D. Whitney, A Sanskrit Grammar, 2nd ed., 1889 (genitive singular of a-stems, §§294–297 for genitive uses)
L. Sternbach (ed.), Mahā-subhāṣita-saṃgraha, no. 3587 (text)

claims.claim: Glosses for saying 3: अष्टादशपुराणेषु 'in the eighteen Purāṇas' (one compound), व्यासस्य 'of Vyāsa', वचनद्वयम् 'a pair of sayings', परोपकारः 'helping others', पुण्याय 'for merit', पापाय 'for sin', परपीडनम् 'harming others' (पीडनम् 'causing pain'). Neither line has a verb; the 'for' endings carry the sense [REF:whitney1889 §287].
claims.evidence: Apte 1890: पर, compound '-उपकारः doing good to others, benevolence…'; पीडनम् '1 Paining, distressing, oppressing, inflicting pain'; वचनम्; द्वयम् 'Pair, couple'; पुण्य 'Good, meritorious, virtuous'; पाप. Whitney §287 covers the dative of end or purpose, and §287a says 'Such a dative is much used predicatively (and oftenest with the copula omitted), in the sense of makes for, tends toward', with a Hitopadeśa example: upadeśo mūrkhāṇām prakopāya na śāntaye. That is exactly the construction of परोपकारः पुण्याय पापाय परपीडनम्. The citation could be sharpened to §287a.

claims.claim: Saying 3 has no joins between words; the visarga of परोपकारः stays a visarga before प्; परोपकारः = पर + उपकारः with अ + उ → ओ [REF:whitney1889 §127; ashtadhyayi 6.1.87].
claims.evidence: No junction in saying 3 needs a change. Vowel before consonant: -eṣu v-, -sya v-, -āya p-. The -m of वचनद्वयम् stands at the half-verse end, in pause. Before p, -ḥ stays visarga (Whitney §170; Pāṇini 8.3.15 खरवसानयोर्विसर्जनीयः). For the join inside परोपकारः, Whitney §127 says 'An a-vowel combines … with an u-vowel, to ओ o', and his own example is hitopadeśaḥ ← hita-upadeśaḥ. Pāṇini 6.1.87 आद्गुणः gives the same rule.
sources: W.D. Whitney, A Sanskrit Grammar, 2nd ed., 1889, §§127, 170
Pāṇini, Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.87, 8.3.15 (ashtadhyayi-com/data)

claims.claim: अष्टादश is one compound numeral, not अष्ट + दश glued by a vowel sandhi; अष्टा- is the shape 'eight' takes in this numeral and a few others [REF:whitney1889 §476].
claims.evidence: Whitney §476 says the odd numbers are made 'by prefixing the (accented) unit to the ten', and §476e: 'aṣṭa becomes aṣṭā (483) in 18–38, and has either form in the succeeding combinations'. §483 calls aṣṭā the older fuller form, used 'both in inflection and in composition', and §475e notes 'The older form of aṣṭa is aṣṭā'. Pāṇini 6.3.47 द्व्यष्टनः संख्यायामबहुव्रीह्यशीत्योः, with आत् carried from 6.3.46 आन्महतः समानाधिकरणजातीययोः, puts ā for the final of aṣṭan before a numeral. No vowel sandhi could produce the ā anyway, because दश begins with a consonant. 'A few others' fits: the ā is obligatory in 28 and 38 and optional from 48 on.
sources: W.D. Whitney, A Sanskrit Grammar, 2nd ed., 1889, §§475e, 476e, 483
Pāṇini, Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.46–47 (ashtadhyayi-com/data)

claims.claim: परपीडनम् is written with plain ड (a retroflex stop), not the Hindi ड़ of पीड़ा.
claims.evidence: Apte has the headword पीडनम् (SLP1 pIqanaM, q = ड): '1 Paining, distressing, oppressing, inflicting pain'. M. Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford 1899, p. 629 s.v. pīḍana

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. The lesson itself contradicts chapter.md's promise. In lesson-03 §4, the table says saying 1 is "an epic, with a locus you can check" and saying 2 is "a fable book, with a locus you can check". It describes saying 3 only as "quoted tradition", with "first line not traced to any Purāṇa".

For saying 3, the lesson cites one source: [REF:apte1890 s.v. पर]. Apte prints only the second line, परोपकारः पुण्याय पापाय परपीडनम्, with no locus, no first line and no mention of Vyāsa. So a reader has nothing to look up for the Vyāsa attribution, which is the core of that source line. The only places the couplet can be found are Sternbach's anthology (MSS 3587) and, for the second line alone, Pañcatantra 3.103 under a different first line. The lesson cites neither; its own metadata says "Sternbach's anthology is not cited (no key)".

I could not refute the finding by reading "sources a reader can check" as "verifiable source lines". "Not traced" is a statement that something is missing, and the lesson itself says it is not proof of absence, so a reader cannot check it either.

The proposed wording is correct and suitably hedged. It repeats the lesson's own wording: "as firm as the evidence and no firmer" (§8), "One phrase, as firm as the evidence" (§13), "the source line is as sure as the evidence" (§26). "Honest source lines" matches objective 2's "one honest phrase".

Each quote occurs exactly once in chapter.md. The replacement lines are 89 and 90 characters, in line with the paragraph's wrapping. They contain no Devanagari parentheses, IPA, REF keys, callouts, the word "descend", or 1.x quotations, so they keep the house rules.

Two lines in sibling lessons make the same overclaim and are not touched by these fixes. They need their own finding or a follow-up:
- lesson-02-the-lion-and-the-mouse.md line 1111 (§26 CTA): "Three real sayings, with sources you can check."
- lesson-05-volume-two-exam.md line 187 (§4): "Chapter 6 gave two famous stories and three sayings checkable sources."

The chapter.md can-do line "...with sources" is looser, but it does not claim the sources can be checked, so it can stay.

KEY FINDINGS
(1) The Hitopadeśa verse number is edition-dependent. Apte 1890's "H." is explicitly the Nirṇaya Sāgara edition, and his "H. Pr. 36" agrees with GRETIL Hit_0.36. But mapping all of Apte's prastāvikā citations onto GRETIL shows the two numberings diverge elsewhere (Pr. 31 = GRETIL 0.33; Pr. 30–32 are reordered; Pr. 41 = 0.40). REFERENCES.md must name a numbering basis. I recommend the GRETIL e-text, which the course already uses for Mitralābha 71 and the cat passage at 1.65. The access note's claim that numbering is "edition-independent" needs a carve-out.
(2) MW does NOT support "chariot of the mind". MW and Böhtlingk–Roth read manoratha as "heart's joy" (2. ratha from √ram), and MW's Additions note a Prakrit-origin theory (mano'rtha). Only Apte has "the car of the mind".
(3) The second line of saying 3 is attested earliest (as far as found) in the textus simplicior Pañcatantra, Book 3 (Jha ed. 3.103). It is spoken by the hypocritical cat Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra under a different first line. The Vyāsa couplet is recorded only as an anthology verse (MSS 3587, vol. II, 1976). No Purāṇa locus was found anywhere, and none is claimed online.
(4) "Two-word essence" mistranslates वचनद्वयम्, which the lesson itself glosses "a pair of sayings".
(5) "This verse ends his reflection" is wrong: three more verses follow (GRETIL 0.37–0.39).

LIMITS
The web-search budget for this turn ran out before the end, so further searches were not possible. archive.org, TITUS, the Sanskrit Library, Wikisource, the Clay Sanskrit Library site, shreevatsa.net, oaks.nvg.org and huggingface.co downloads are blocked from this session. - Pūrṇabhadra's Sanskrit wording. The verse is attested there only via Ryder's English translation.
- The Vikramacarita variant (from a blog report).
The textus simplicior bracket c. 900–1199 comes from a secondary snippet (Penzer, vol. 5, App. I); it is for internal use only and should not go into lessons.

topics.topic: Word Journeys: cognates, loans, Latin/Greek-route words, false etymologies and modern coinages (v2.c06.l04, its restatements in l05 and chapter.md, loan mentions in l03)

claims.claim: Grimm's Law as the §5 FACT callout states it: where Sanskrit and Latin keep p, t and d, the inherited English word shows f, th and t; where Sanskrit has bh and dh, English shows b and d; Latin did not take part in that shift.
claims.evidence: The core is right. Grimm's Law (the First Germanic Sound Shift) turned the PIE voiceless stops into fricatives (*p > f, *t > þ, *k > h), the voiced stops into voiceless ones (*d > t), and the breathy-voiced stops into plain voiced ones (*bʰ > b, *dʰ > d). Latin stands outside the shift; its own change made initial *bʰ- into f-, as in frāter. The callout, however, states the rule with no exceptions, and the standard formulation has two that bite this lesson. (1) A voiceless stop right after *s, or after another obstruent, did not shift: PIE *st and *kt stay st and ht. That gives √स्था ~ stāre ~ stand, नक्त ~ noct- ~ night and अष्ट ~ octō ~ eight. (2) Verner's Law voiced the new fricatives in some positions: *ph₂tḗr gave Old English fæder, with d. Two of the lesson's own fifteen cognate rows (stand, night) therefore show t ~ t, not t ~ th, and a learner applying the unqualified rule would wrongly reject true cognates. The ladder rows are chosen to avoid both exceptions and are themselves correct (WJ-02).
sources: D. Ringe, From Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic (A Linguistic History of English, vol. 1), Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006; 2nd ed. 2017, §3.2.4 'Grimm's Law and Verner's Law' (section number from the published table of contents; pages not re-checked)
J.P. Mallory & D.Q. Adams, The Oxford Introduction to Proto-Indo-European and the Proto-Indo-European World, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006 (cognate sets)
Wikipedia, 'Grimm's law', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimm%27s_law (three phases; no shift after *s or after another obstruent; Verner's law)
claims.correct_wording: Between Sanskrit, Latin and English the best-known set is the Germanic consonant shift (Grimm's Law): where Sanskrit and Latin keep p, t and d, the inherited English word as a rule shows f, th and t (a t right after s or k stays t: stand, night); where Sanskrit has bh and dh, English shows b and d. Latin did not take part in that shift. [REF:mallory2006]; [REF:burrow2001] (optionally add [REF:ringe2006 §3.2.4], proposed below)

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding: the problem is real and the fix is correct. The §5 FACT callout (lines 174-179) gives the shift as a rule with no exceptions: where Sanskrit and Latin keep t, English shows th. The lesson's own §13 FACT callout (lines 504-507) lists नक्त ~ night as cognates. Sanskrit nakta has t, Latin noctis has t, and English night also has t, because a t right after another stop did not shift in Germanic (Proto-Germanic *nahts). So a learner who applies §5 to §13 would reject a pair the lesson says is cognate. Latin stāre ~ stand (t ~ t) is the same case: Germanic kept *st. Saying "as a rule" and naming the s/k exception is accurate. It respects the house rules, the quote occurs exactly once, and the validator passes.

One small adjustment. In the researcher's wording, "stand" sits in a clause that starts "where Sanskrit and Latin keep t". But Sanskrit स्था (sthā) has an aspirated th there, not a plain t. And bare "night" hides the k. Giving the Latin forms (stāre ~ stand, noctis ~ night) shows the st and ct clusters and matches the clause's premise.

Notes:
(1) The Verner's Law point is only background. Old English fæder and mōdor had d, but modern father and mother have th again through a later d > th change before -er. No modern word in the lesson contradicts the rule, so "as a rule" covers it, and no Verner clause should be added (the proposal adds none).
(2) The bh/dh clause is also simplified: between vowels, bh appears in English as v (नाभि ~ navel). No such pair appears anywhere in the course, so hedging it is optional.
(3) ringe2006 is not in REFERENCES.md. The fix does not add it, so it is valid as it stands. If the source is cited later, it needs a REFERENCES.md entry first and a checked locator; I could not confirm §3.2.4.
(4) After editing, re-run scripts/export_json.py. export_json.py --check marks json/volume-2/v2.c06.l04.json (line 338) out of date until it is regenerated.
challenge.better_wording: Between Sanskrit, Latin and English the best-known set is the Germanic consonant shift (Grimm's Law): where Sanskrit and Latin keep *p*, *t* and *d*, the inherited English word as a rule shows *f*, *th* and *t* (a *t* right after *s* or *k* stays *t*: Latin *stāre* ~ *stand*, *noctis* ~ *night*); where Sanskrit has *bh* and *dh*, English shows *b* and *d*. Latin did not take part in that shift. [REF:mallory2006]; [REF:burrow2001]. No new REF key is needed. If [REF:ringe2006] is added later, create its REFERENCES.md entry first and check the § locator, which is unconfirmed. Re-run scripts/export_json.py after the edit.

claims.claim: The shift ladder (§5) and its restatements: पादः·pēs·foot p~p~f, d~d~t; पितृ·pater·father p~p~f; दन्तः·dēns·tooth d~d~t; द्वि·duo·two d~d~t; त्रि·trēs·three t~t~th; भ्रातृ·frāter·brother bh~f~b; मध्यम्·medius·mid dh~d~d; विधवा·vidua·widow dh~d~d. Latin kept p and d and English shifted them, so the Latin-route words look closer (Q7, Exercise 5).
claims.evidence: Every rung matches the standard reconstructions: *pṓds > Skt pā́d-, Lat. pēs/pedis, PGmc *fōts > OE fōt; *ph₂tḗr > pitár-, pater, OE fæder (the row prints only p~p~f and so rightly avoids father's Verner d); *h₁dónts > dánt-, dēns, OE tōþ; *dwóh₁ > dvā́/dvi-, duo, OE twā; *tréyes > tráyaḥ/tri-, trēs, OE þrīe; *bʰréh₂tēr > bhrā́tar-, frāter (Latin f- from initial *bʰ-), OE brōþor; *médʰyos > mádhya-, medius (Latin medial *dʰ > d), OE midd; *h₁widʰéwh₂ > vidhávā, vidua, OE widuwe. The Exercise 5 Part B key (pedal or pedestrian, dental, triple, fraternal, medium or median) lists only Latin-derived English words. The explanation 'Latin kept the old consonants that English shifted' is accurate.

claims.evidence: Grimm's Law changed the manner of articulation, not the place of contact. A stop (full closure, then release) became a fricative (air streaming through a narrow gap without a break). For PIE *p the Germanic fricative was probably bilabial [ɸ] at first and became labiodental [f] later, so the lip-to-teeth contact is a secondary development. In the shift's other half (d → t, as in दन्तः ~ tooth) the contact does not change at all; only voicing does. Calling the shift 'that small change of contact' teaches the wrong mechanism. The difference worth feeling in the drill is closure-and-release against an unbroken hiss.

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. In Grimm's Law, *p → f is a change in manner of articulation: a voiceless stop (full closure, then release) became a voiceless fricative (air flowing without a break through a narrow gap). The check names only the place difference (lip on lip versus lip on teeth) and calls "that small change of contact" the shift. It even suggests f is just another closure ("meets"). So the learner feels the wrong mechanism. The lesson's own ladder shows why the place reading fails. In त्रि ~ three (t ~ th) the place stays dental and only stop → fricative changes. In दन्तः ~ tooth (d ~ t) only voicing changes. The labiodental place of modern English f is incidental; the Proto-Germanic sound is usually reconstructed as bilabial [ɸ]. That point is rightly hedged as "probably" and the wording does not need it.

The proposed wording correctly moves the drill to closure-and-release against air that never stops. It matches the course's existing FACT definition of a fricative (v1.c04.l02 §5, [REF:ladefoged2015]: "where a stop makes full closure, a fricative leaves a narrow channel") and its "hiss" wording for [f] (v1.c03.l05). It keeps the house rules: no IPA, no parenthesis after a Devanagari word, no REF needed outside a callout, no time-depth figure.

One adjustment is needed. The proposal keeps "is the shift of §5", but §5's FACT box defines the shift as p, t → f, th, plus d → t, plus bh, dh → b, d. A stop becoming a hiss is only one part of that. The researcher's own evidence says the d → t part changes only voicing, so the sentence should say "one part of the shift". The same wrong mechanism also appears in §24 ("a lip diagram shows the contact change"), and §23's mouth strip shows only the places. Both should be updated so the lesson stays consistent.

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding. English ignite is not formed from the noun ignis. It is formed on ignīt-, the participle stem of the Latin verb ignīre "set on fire", and ignīre is in turn built on ignis. The "-ite" ending is the Latin participle ending -ītus (compare unite from ūnīt-), so the English form cannot come from ignis alone.

The course's own research dossier records exactly this chain. The §13 table writes the same kind of chain for other rows ("from Latin duālis, from duo", "from Late Latin nocturnālis, from nox"), so a one-step "from Latin ignis" reads as if ignis were the direct source. The Exercise 2 key ("ignite came from Latin ignis") makes the same misstatement.

The proposed fix is accurate and small. It keeps ignis, the actual cognate of अग्निः, in view, and it matches standard dictionary practice of citing the Latin verb by its infinitive, as Collins and the American Heritage Dictionary do.

Caveats, none of which blocks the fix:
1. Low severity. The kind-(c) label and the अग्निः ~ ignis cognacy were already right; only the immediate etymon was wrong.
2. The researcher's consistency argument is selective. The dental row (from Medieval Latin dentālis) and the pedal/pedestrian row (from Latin pedālis / pedester) are shortened the same way. The table is therefore mixed, but that does not make the ignite row accurate. Those rows are outside this finding and may deserve the same treatment.
3. The OED treats the verb as partly an English conversion of the old adjective ignite (from Latin ignītus). "From Latin ignīre" is the usual dictionary shorthand and is fine at this level; the route is Latin either way.
4. The sentence at line 548 ("the English word's parent is the Latin or Greek word, and that parent is Sanskrit's sibling") was already loose for dual, nocturnal and novel. After the fix, ignite simply joins those rows; no new contradiction is created.
5. Minor: the researcher calls it the "route" column, but the column is headed "The honest line".

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. The sentence says "In every case the English word's parent is the Latin or Greek word". But the sentence right before it says *state*, *station* and *voice* came "through Old French" and *novel* "through Italian and Old French". The §13 callout says *serpent* came "through Old French", and *pedal* (the noun) came through French and Italian. So read as a parent relation, the universal is contradicted by its own paragraph.

Where the source is Latin, it is usually a derivative: dentālis, pedālis, pedester, triplus, duālis, nocturnālis, vōcālis, novellus, ignīre. The word that is cognate with the Sanskrit one is the base. So "that parent is Sanskrit's sibling" is false for most rows.

A third reason, which the researcher did not raise: elsewhere the course uses "parent and child" as its metaphor for descent ("siblings, not parent and child — all descend from one reconstructed ancestor"; "two children of one ancient parent"). Here that language is applied to a borrowing, which goes against the rule that descent wording is kept for cognacy. It also makes the English word the Sanskrit word's niece or nephew, which contradicts the section's own label, "Cousins through Latin and Greek".

The proposed replacement fixes all of this and is mostly accurate. But "a Latin or Greek word built on a cognate" fails for *voice*, whose Latin source vōx is itself the cognate of वाच्, not something built on it. It also clashes with the §13 callouts, which name serpēns and vidēre as the cognates themselves. Changing it to "that is, or is built on, a cognate" makes the universal true for every row.

The fix quote occurs exactly once (line 548, on one line). The replacement adds no Devanagari, IPA, REF key, quotation marks, time-depth figure or "descend". The preceding [REF:oed s.vv.] key exists in REFERENCES.md, and the file has no wrap or line-length lint.
challenge.better_wording: In every case the English word's history runs back, often through French or Italian, to a Latin or Greek word that is, or is built on, a cognate of the Sanskrit one.
