challenge.reason: The problem is real but small. The substance of both key lines is right: the direction (not from Sanskrit), cognacy, the kind-(c) Latin route and the March-first Roman year. The wording is literally wrong, though. English October and November are the Latin month names Octōber and November, which are built on the numerals octō "eight" and novem "nine". "X is Latin octō/novem" says the month name is the numeral. Card 3 is worse: it gives no "eight" gloss, and its appositive "the eighth month of the old Roman year" sits on octō, so it reads as glossing octō as "the eighth month". That phrase belongs to the Latin month name (compare Merriam-Webster's form: "from Latin October, eighth month of the early Roman calendar, from octo eight"). This matters in this chapter because the course defines kind (c) as an English word from Latin "whose root is cognate with a Sanskrit word" (notes §0.9; exam Station 0: "reached English from Latin, whose root is cognate with a Sanskrit one"). The key merges the borrowed word and the cognate root, which are exactly the two things that definition keeps apart. It is also looser than the source it cites, v2.c03.l02 §13 ("naming the 8th, 9th and 10th months"). The strongest counter-argument is that this is common shorthand and appears in the reviewed v2.c03.l05 Q3 key ("November is Latin's own novem 'nine', counting the ninth month"). That key at least keeps a naming verb; the c06 key drops it, and c06 is still a draft under review. The proposed wording is accurate and needs no hedge. claims.claim: विमानम् is a classical word from वि + √मा 'measure out, traverse', whose classical senses include the gods' aerial car, a palace and a temple tower, given the modern sense 'aeroplane'. मान means 'measure' or 'honour, pride', never 'vehicle'. Glossing वि as 'special' is loose but has traditional precedent; its basic senses are 'apart, out'. Exam keys: '(a measuring-out, then the gods' aerial car in epic poetry)'.
claims.evidence: MW vimāna, from vi-√mā 'to measure, mete out, pass over, traverse' (RV): adjective 'measuring out, traversing' (RV); m. 'a measure', 'extension' (RV); m./n. 'a car or chariot of the gods, any mythical self-moving aerial car (… sometimes like a house or palace, one kind 7 stories high)' (MBh., Kāv.); 'any car or vehicle (esp. a bier)'; 'the palace of an emperor (esp. one with 7 stories)'; 'a temple or shrine of a particular form'; 'a ship, boat'; 'a horse'. The lesson's senses (aerial car, palace, temple tower) and the exam's Vedic-then-epic ordering match MW. For māna: Apte gives n. (from √mā) 'measuring; a measure, standard, dimension'; MW and Apte give m. (from √man) 'opinion … self-conceit, pride; honour, respect'. Neither has a 'vehicle' sense, so the 1.x gloss is false. Apte s.v. vi lists '(d) distinction, as विशिष्, विशेष' among the prefix's senses, which supports 'loose but has traditional precedent'; its basic sense is 'apart, asunder'. 'वि + √मा gives विमान' leaves out the kṛt suffix -ana, an acceptable simplification at this level. Apte's own vimāna headword could not be retrieved, but MW suffices for the cited [REF:monierwilliams1899 s.v. विमान].

claims.claim: आकाशवाणी is display-only (आकाश 'sky' + वाणी 'voice', India's public radio; the 1.x gloss sky-voice was right). Who first proposed the name for radio is disputed, so the course names no one and gives no date.

Gopalaswamy, whose private Mysore station (1935/36) was called 'Akashvani' and who is the person AIR Mysore officially recognises; Rabindranath Tagore, whose poem 'Akashvani' marked the 1938 Calcutta short-wave inauguration; the poet Narendra Sharma (on Wikipedia-derived pages); Hosbet Rama Rao (a 1932 booklet); and Rallapalli Ananta Krishna Sharma (Wikipedia). AIR adopted the name in 1956 (some sources say 1957), and since 2023 it has been the only name used on air. In this chapter the word appears only in l04: the §13 bullet, the §14 display-only list and the §27 notes. It is absent from l05 and chapter.md. claims.claim: Building words from parts is something 'every language does' (§12 item 7) and 'हर भाषा में आम है' (objective 4, Hindi).
claims.evidence: The true core is that word-building from parts is ordinary across languages, which is the phrasing of the English objective 4 and Q9 ('a method many languages use'). 'Every language' is an unsourced scale claim (STYLE_GUIDE §7), and typologists do not agree on it. Derivational affixation is minimal in strongly isolating languages. Even compounding is not agreed to be universal: Bauer (2017) concludes that no agreement on its universality is possible, Pepper (2020) argues noun-noun compounding is not universal, and one cross-linguistic sample finds compounding in about 91% of its languages.
sources: L. Bauer, Compounds and Compounding (Cambridge Studies in Linguistics 155), Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2017
S. Pepper, 'The typology of binominal lexemes', DGfS 2020 AG 4 abstract, https://www.zfs.uni-hamburg.de/dgfs2020/programm/abstracts/dgfs2020-ag04-pepper.pdf
R. Lieber & P. Štekauer (eds), The Oxford Handbook of Compounding, Oxford: OUP, 2009
claims.correct_wording: Saying only Sanskrit can build words from parts. Many languages do; tele-vision and Fern-seh-er are built the same way. (Hindi objective: हिस्से जोड़कर शब्द बनाना बहुत-सी भाषाओं में आम है।)

challenge.reason:
I tried to refute the finding and could not. "Every language does" (§12 item 7) and "हर भाषा में आम है" (Hindi objective 4) are universal claims about all languages, with no source. STYLE_GUIDE §7 says "Claims of scale carry numbers with sources or don't appear." The lesson's only support is two examples, English and German. The lesson also contradicts itself: English objective 4 says "ordinary across languages", the Q9 key says "a method many languages use", §8 says "Neither method is unique to Sanskrit", and the §7 Hindi says "केवल संस्कृत की कोई अनोखी प्रतिभा नहीं". So the Hindi objective is also a mistranslation of its own English twin: "ordinary across languages" became "common in every language". The chapter's own research dossier advised against exactly this: "use English examples, which are self-evident, rather than a scale claim", with suggested wording "Many languages work like this".

My strongest counter-argument partly lands but does not save the original. The researcher's evidence takes compounding and derivation one at a time. It shows neither is clearly universal, but it does not show a language that has neither. So "typologists do not agree on it" is aimed at compounding, not at word-building in general, which may in fact be close to universal. Even so, no source in hand establishes that. "Every language" stays an unsourced universal, and a debunking passage should not swap one overclaim ("only Sanskrit") for another.

The fix itself is minimal and correct:
- "Many languages do" is true from the lesson's own examples and matches the Q9 key that §12 item 7 feeds.
- "बहुत-सी" with a hyphen is the form the chapter already uses (lessons 1 and 2).
- Each quoted string occurs exactly once.
- No IAST, IPA, REF or callout rules are affected.
- The validator passes on a patched copy.

None of the unverified typology details (Bauer's conclusion, Pepper's abstract, the ~91% figure) get printed, so the fix does not depend on them.

claims.claim: 'English built television from Greek tele- and Latin vision' (§8); Exercise 6 key: 'Greek tele- + Latin vision'.

where.section: §8 Two honest kinds of modern word

claims.evidence: There is no Latin word 'vision'. The element is English vision, from (Old) French vision < Latin vīsiō 'seeing'. The first part is Greek tēle 'far'. That English coined the word is also contested. The French télévision was first used by Constantin Perskyi in a paper read at the International Electricity Congress in Paris on 25 August 1900; English television is recorded from 1907. Etymonline says it was 'formed in English or borrowed from French télévision'. The OED supplement is reported (Wiktionary talk page, not seen directly) to analyse it as tele- + vision. The point of the passage, that the word is built from a Greek and a Latin-derived part, survives a neutral wording.
sources: Etymonline, 'television', https://www.etymonline.com/word/television
Wiktionary, 'television', https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/television (first attestation 1900; Perskyi's French télévision)
claims.correct_wording: Neither method is unique to Sanskrit — television was built from Greek tēle 'far' and vision (from Latin vīsiō), and German built Fern-seh-er from 'far', 'see' and a doer-suffix. Exercise 6 (e): Greek tēle 'far' + vision (from Latin vīsiō) — built from parts in another language.

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. "Latin *vision*" names a word Latin never had: the Latin noun is vīsiō (accusative vīsiōnem), and *vision* is the English (and French) form. The lesson holds itself to a stricter standard everywhere else. It gives real Latin forms with macrons (*dēns, dentis*, *serpēns*, *videō*, *vōx*, *ioculārī*). Its kind (c) test also depends on keeping an English word apart from its Latin source ("English got the word from Latin"). So labelling an English word as Latin contradicts the lesson's own method. The slip appears twice: once in §8 prose and once in the Exercise 6 answer key, which students mark themselves against.

"English built *television*" is also an overclaim. French *télévision* (Perskyi, Paris, 1900) is older than English *television* (1907), and Etymonline hedges between "formed in English" and "borrowed from French". The proposed passive, "*television* was built from…", is true whichever story is right, and it makes no claim about who coined the word.

The rest of the proposal is accurate and keeps the house rules:
- τῆλε does mean "far off".
- English *vision* does come, through Old French, from Latin vīsiō.
- No parenthesis follows a Devanagari word, and there is no IPA, no "descend", no 1.x text in quotation marks and no time-depth figure.
- No REF is needed in §8 prose. The researcher was right not to add an [REF:oed] they had not seen.
- Each quote occurs exactly once, and the edited file passes scripts/validate.py.

One refinement (optional, for consistency): use *têle* rather than *tēle*. Every other Greek form in this lesson carries its accent, with the circumflex written as ^ (*hṓra*, *thygátēr*, *gnôsis*, *zygón*, *oîda*), and τῆλε written that way is *têle*. *tēle* (Etymonline's spelling) is not wrong, so the better_fixes below differ from the proposal only in that one spelling.

Out of scope:
- §13 line 594, "English builds *un-break-able* and *tele-vision*", is a general present-tense statement about English word structure and can stand.
- §7 (Hindi), §12 mistake 7, quiz key 9, the FACT callout and the video and voice-over scripts give no Latin label and need no change.
- json/volume-2/v2.c06.l04.json carries the same text. It should be regenerated with scripts/export_json.py after the markdown edit, not edited by hand (CONTRIBUTING.md: markdown is the source of truth).
challenge.better_wording: Neither method is unique to Sanskrit — *television* was built from Greek *têle* "far" and *vision* (from Latin *vīsiō*), and German built *Fern-seh-er* from "far", "see" and a doer-suffix. Exercise 6 (e): Greek *têle* "far" + *vision* (from Latin *vīsiō*) — built from parts in another language. (Identical to the researcher's proposal except *têle* for *tēle*, to match this lesson's accent-marked Greek: *hṓra*, *gnôsis*, *oîda*. After the edit, regenerate the JSON mirror with scripts/export_json.py.)

claims.claim: 'Modern Sanskrit makes new words in two ways, and the course labels both' (calques; old words with new jobs).

where.section: §8 Two honest kinds of modern word

claims.evidence: The two kinds the lesson labels are real. But modern Sanskrit also coins compounds and derivatives with no foreign model, and occasionally takes loanwords. The lesson contradicts 'two ways' itself: its Exercise 6 key labels संगणक neither a calque nor an old word with a new job, but a 'modern word from classical parts'.
sources: curriculum/volume-2/chapter-06/lesson-04-word-journeys.md §19, Exercise 6 key (internal evidence)
Source research, cognates topic (research/evidence/vol2-ch6-source-research.json): the 1.x technology list mixes calques and classical words with new meanings, plus other coinages
claims.correct_wording: Modern Sanskrit makes new words in several ways, and the course labels the two met here.

challenge.reason: The problem is real. "Modern Sanskrit makes new words in two ways" is a plain, present-tense claim that those two ways are the only ones. A calque, as the lesson itself defines it, needs a foreign model translated part by part. So the claim leaves out new compounds and derivatives built with no foreign model, and it leaves out borrowing and hybrid words. The course's own material points the same way: (1) The Exercise 6 key gives संगणक a label that is neither of the two ("modern word from classical parts"), and the §13 FACT callout avoids calling it a calque. (2) The source research's corrected quiz key says modern words are built from classical parts "often translating the English word part by part": often, not always. (3) v1.c06.l01 presents विद्यालयः, "abode of learning", as standard modern usage built from classical parts, and that compound translates no English word. (4) This same lesson keeps होरा as a reminder that Sanskrit also takes words in. The proposed wording drops the claim that the list is complete. "Several" is safely vague and adds no unsourced figure. The new text still matches the heading ("Two honest kinds") and the next sentence ("Neither method..."), and it agrees with Objective 4. "The two met here" follows house usage (compare "the pair met in v1.c06.l03" in v2.c04.l04). The quote occurs exactly once. The replacement adds no Devanagari, parentheses, IPA, REF, callout, "descend" or quotation marks. One caveat: the researcher's summary of the source research ("plus other coinages") overstates it. Its notes sort the 1.x technology list into exactly two types. That supports "the two met here" and does not undercut the fix. The Exercise 6 key's off-menu label for संगणक is a separate issue that already existed and is outside this fix.

claims.claim: The 1.x unit credited word-building to a special 'genius' of Sanskrit (paraphrased, not quoted). The building is real, the uniqueness is not; Sanskrit has a large, highly productive system and a grammatical tradition that described it in unusual detail [REF:cardona1997].
claims.evidence: The 1.x PDF p. 63 quiz reads 'The genius of Sanskrit: you can create new words by: … Combining roots + prefixes + suffixes ✓'. The lesson paraphrases it without quotation marks, as the house rule requires. That Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī derives words explicitly from roots, upasargas, kṛt and taddhita suffixes and compounding, in exceptional detail, is the standard scholarly assessment set out in Cardona 1997. The sentence makes no 'unique' or 'most scientific' claim.
sources: Sanskritam-Curriculum.pdf (1.x), p. 63
G. Cardona, Pāṇini: His Work and its Traditions, 2nd ed., Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1997

claims.claim: Hindi दाँत, पाँव and साँप are tadbhava forms of these Sanskrit words (l04 §7, §22). l04 §27 flags this for checking against masica1991, or softening.
claims.evidence: Turner's Comparative Dictionary, as cited by Wiktionary: Hindi दाँत (dā̃t) < Prakrit daṃta < Skt dánta (s.v. dánta, p. 352); Hindi पाँव (pā̃v) < Śaurasenī Prakrit pāa < Skt pā́da (s.v. pā́da, p. 455); Hindi साँप (sā̃p) < Śaurasenī Prakrit sappa (with compensatory lengthening and nasalization) < Skt sarpá (s.v. sarpá). Hindi पैर is a separate derivative (s.v. *padara-). The traditional tadbhava description in §7 is accurate. Turner, not Masica, is the right source if a citation is added; see new_references.
sources: R.L. Turner, A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages, London: OUP, 1962–1966, s.vv. dánta (p. 352), pā́da (p. 455), sarpá, as cited by Wiktionary 'दाँत' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%A6%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%81%E0%A4%A4), 'پاؤں' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%BE%D8%A7%D8%A4%DA%BA) and 'साँप' (https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%81%E0%A4%AA)

claims.claim: 'Every English word has a recorded route, and today the routes are the whole story.' (§4)
claims.evidence: Historical dictionaries mark a number of common English words as of unknown or uncertain origin (dog, boy and girl are the textbook cases), so not every English word has a recorded route. The lesson's own homework concedes that most words have no Sanskrit connection at all. This item was not re-checked by web search: the shared search budget ran out before it could be. It rests on standard dictionary knowledge.
sources: Oxford English Dictionary online, s.vv. dog, boy, girl ('origin uncertain/unknown'); not re-searched in this run
claims.correct_wording: Most English words have a recorded route, and today the routes are the whole story.

challenge.reason:
The overclaim is real, and the course contradicts itself. v1.c03.l05 §13 has an audited FACT callout saying that where English *path* came from "is uncertain", citing [REF:oed s.v. path]. One cited counterexample is enough to sink "Every English word has a recorded route." The textbook cases the researcher names (dog, boy, girl, labelled as of unknown or uncertain origin in the standard historical dictionaries) point the same way.

The proposed "Most English words have a recorded route, and today the routes are the whole story." is accurate and hedged about right. "Most" is a plain quantifier, not one of the banned unsourced percentages. The sentence still sets up the lesson's route-first sort, and nothing else in the lesson or its quiz depends on the universal.

Mechanics:
- The fix quote occurs exactly once in its file (line 136, plain ASCII).
- The replacement applies cleanly in a dry run on a scratch copy.
- It breaks no house rule. It is plain prose outside any callout, with no Devanagari, IPA, REF, "descend" or quotation marks, and it needed no REF before either.

Two caveats:
- The researcher's homework argument proves nothing. A word with no Sanskrit connection can still have a recorded route, so it adds no support. The finding stands on the counterexamples.
- I could not re-check online. The shared WebSearch budget was used up, and etymonline.com and oed.com are outside this session's allowed network domains. The verdict rests on the course's own audited OED citation for *path* plus standard dictionary knowledge for dog, boy and girl.

claims.claim: §4 FACT: English is in the Germanic branch and Sanskrit in the Indo-Iranian branch; words both inherited are cognates; English borrowed widely from Latin, French and Greek; its oldest everyday words (mother, foot, tooth, night, widow) were inherited.
claims.evidence: This is standard. Sanskrit sits in the Indo-Aryan subgroup of Indo-Iranian. All five example words are PIE-inherited (WJ-04, WJ-06, WJ-07). 'The dictionary records each borrowed word's route' is broadly true, though the OED is sometimes tentative (video 'apparently'; yogi 'multiple origins').
sources: J.P. Mallory & D.Q. Adams 2006 (as above)
Oxford English Dictionary online, s.vv. video, yogi

claims.claim: Exam and chapter restatements of the four kinds: the l05 §15 FACT direction toolkit (cognate / loan both ways / Latin route with video, serpent, dental, October / false); task D cards 2, 7, 8 and their verdicts; Q9; §12 rows 3–4; §21 homework 4; chapter.md ('video, ignite and serpent came to English through Latin, and juggle is unrelated to yoke'; can-do on video vs yoga vs juggle).
claims.evidence: The kind assignments all hold: mother cognate; yoga and karma loans from Sanskrit; होरा a loan from Greek; video, serpent, dental and October Latin-route; juggle false. The definition 'reached English from Latin, whose root is cognate' is precise (serpent's Old French step is still the Latin route). Card verdicts 2 FACT, 7 reject and 8 FACT are correct. Two wording issues in the l05 keys are handled elsewhere: the videō source (WJ-14) and the month-name phrasing (WJ-31). 'Descent' is used only of cognacy.

new_references_proposed.entry: **ringe2006** — D. Ringe, *From Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic* (A Linguistic History of English, vol. 1), Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2006; 2nd ed. 2017. Grimm's Law and Verner's Law: §3.2.4. Cited by §.
new_references_proposed.why: An optional citation for the qualified Grimm's Law statement in l04 §5 (no shift after s or another obstruent; Verner's Law) and for the stop-to-fricative mechanism behind the §11 mouth check (WJ-01, WJ-03). REFERENCES.md has no source on Germanic historical phonology; mallory2006 and burrow2001 cover cognate sets, not the conditions on the shift.

new_references_proposed.entry: **turner1966** — R.L. Turner, *A Comparative Dictionary of the Indo-Aryan Languages*, London: Oxford University Press, 1962–1966; Indexes (comp. D.R. Turner), 1969; Phonetic Analysis, 1971; Addenda and Corrigenda (ed. J.C. Wright), 1985. Online at Digital Dictionaries of South Asia (dsal.uchicago.edu). Cited s.v. the Old Indo-Aryan headword, e.g. `[REF:turner1966 s.v. dánta]`.
new_references_proposed.why: The standard etymological source for the Hindi tadbhava descent claimed in l04 §7 and §22 (दाँत < dánta, पाँव < pā́da, साँप < sarpá; WJ-42). The §27 flag points to masica1991, but Masica is a typology; Turner is the dictionary that documents these chains.

topics.notes:
Most of the word-journey content holds. All 15 cognate rows, the Latin- and Greek-route cognacy links, juggle as a false pair, the योग/युग split, the vimāna etymology, the मान correction, the calque labels and the आकाशवाणी hedge are correct. Fifteen items need a fix:

(1) Yoga's first attestation (WJ-11). The online OED, which REFERENCES.md names as [REF:oed], now gives 1785: Charles Wilkins's Bhagavad Gītā, spelled 'Yōg'. Merriam-Webster also gives 1785. 'c. 1820' is the OED1/NED date (Ward 1820) and Etymonline's. yogi is 1613 (Purchas), so 'recorded earlier' stands. dharma and karma are both 1785 (Wilkins) in the OED, borrowed directly from Sanskrit; no lesson dates them.

(2) video (WJ-14). The OED gives Latin vidēre + connective -o-; Merriam-Webster, Random House and Collins agree ('as in audio'). Only Etymonline gives videō 'I see'. There are nine places across l04 and l05.

(3) 'The one word on today's list that English truly borrowed' (WJ-12). English also has vimana (OED, from 1863).

(4) Grimm's Law (WJ-01, WJ-03). The rule is stated without its t-after-s/k exception, which the lesson's own stand and night rows violate. §11 also describes the shift as a change of contact when it is a stop becoming a fricative.

claims.claim: l02 §14 glosses कृन्तति as 'cuts, gnaws through' in English and 'काटता है, कुतरता है' in Hindi.
claims.evidence: Apte 420a: kṛt 6 P. (kṛntati) 'To cut, cut off, divide, tear asunder, cut in pieces, destroy'. MW 304,2: 'to cut, cut in pieces, cut off, divide, tear asunder, destroy'. Neither dictionary gives 'gnaw'. Gnawing is what the mouse does with the verb in this story, not the verb's meaning. Elsewhere the lesson glosses it correctly: §8 'cuts', §17 line 10 'He cuts through the net', and l05 §14 'cuts'.
sources: Apte 1890 s.v. कृत्, p. 420a (Cologne AP90)
Monier-Williams 1899 s.v. 2. kṛt, p. 304, cols 2–3 (Cologne MW)
claims.correct_wording: कृन्तति: 'cuts, cuts through' (काटता है). In the story the mouse cuts with his teeth, which Hindi calls कुतरता है.

challenge.reason: The problem is real. Every standard dictionary I checked gives √कृत् 6P (kṛntati) only senses of cutting. The verbs that do carry "gnaw" are other roots: Apte gives it under √rad and vi-√ad, MW under kuṣ, rad, vy-ad and pari-rih, and Böhtlingk lists "-nagen" under √chid. The English–Sanskrit dictionaries render "gnaw" with daṃś or carv. Where they use kṛt at all, the gnawing comes from an added instrument word, as in Apte's "carvaṇena kṛt" ("cut by chewing"). So "gnaws through" and कुतरता है describe the mouse's action in the story, not what the verb means. That makes them an overclaim in a §14 row. These rows are exported to the lesson JSON (json/volume-2/v2.c06.l02.json), where the story context is lost. The row is also the outlier. The other verb rows in the same table are backed by Apte (grah "seize, take, catch"; muc "release, let go"; baddha "captured, caught"). Every other gloss of कृन्तति in the chapter says "cuts" or काटता है: §6, §7, §8 and its FACT callout, §17 line 10, the l04 riddle "अहम् फलम् कृन्तामि" ("I cut the fruit"), and l05 §14. The proposed fix is correct. "cuts, cuts through" matches §17's "He cuts through the net" and the dictionary senses "divide, tear asunder" and "cut in pieces". काटता है is the right Hindi. The note keeps the point about teeth and uses the same कुतरना that §7's Hindi already uses for gnawing. It follows the house rules: no parenthesis directly after a Devanagari word, no new REF needed because §8's callout already cites apte1890 s.v. कृत् and monierwilliams1899 s.v. kṛt, and no IPA change. The quote occurs exactly once. No changes are needed to the proposal.

claims.claim: l04 presents पादः 'foot' and पद 'step; word' as two meanings told apart by vowel length ('Length is meaning here'; 'पद कदम या शब्द'; 'not पद "step; word"').
claims.evidence: The first sense of पदम् in Apte (663a) is '1 A foot (said to be m. also in this sense)'. MW 583,1 gives pada n. 'a step, pace, stride; a footstep, trace, vestige, mark, the foot itself, RV. &c.'. पाद is 'the foot' in both (Apte 693b; MW 617,1), and neither lists 'step' or 'word' for it. So पद and पादः are two words from one root, but both can mean 'foot'. Vowel length tells the words apart; it does not by itself separate 'step' from 'foot'. The Q1 key ('(b) is पद, a different word') and §12 mistake 9 stay correct.
sources: Apte 1890 s.v. पदम्, p. 663a, and s.v. पादः, p. 693b (Cologne AP90)
Monier-Williams 1899 s.v. pada, p. 583,1, and s.v. pāda, p. 617,1 (Cologne MW)
claims.correct_wording: पादः 'foot' and पद 'step, footprint; word' (sometimes also 'foot') are two different words from one root, √पद्. The long आ tells you which word you have.

challenge.reason: I could not refute the finding. Two passages in l04 tie vowel length to a step-versus-foot difference in meaning. The §7 Hindi line says "पादः पैर है, पद कदम या शब्द", and §9 Drill 2 says "Length is meaning here: a step, a foot". But पद (pada) n. can itself mean 'foot': MW gives "a step, pace, stride; a footstep, trace, vestige, mark, the foot itself, RV. &c." (with padena 'on foot'), and Apte gives "A foot" as the first sense of पदम्. Hindi has the same use in पदयात्रा and पदचिह्न, which Hindi-speaking learners already know. So the long आ tells two words apart (pada vs pāda, a real minimal pair); it does not separate 'step' from 'foot'. That makes this an overclaim, not a plain error. The course's own source dossier hedged it ("पद (pada) is MAINLY 'step, footprint, position; word'"), and the lesson dropped the hedge. The Q1 key, §12 mistake 9 and §13's "the closer match is पाद" stay correct. The proposed wording is accurate and properly hedged, and fixes 2 and 3 are fine. Two fixes need changes. Fix 1 puts a Hindi parenthetical right after Devanagari words ("…निशान या शब्द (कभी-कभी पैर भी)"), which breaks the stated rule that such a parenthesis holds only that word's IAST. Fix 4 names "Apte" in bare prose with no [REF:] tag, and it suggests only Apte has the sense when MW gives it too. Corrected versions are below; all four quotes occur exactly once.

claims.claim: l04 labels दूरदर्शनम् flatly as a modern word ('MODERN', 'a modern calque', Hindi 'आधुनिक शब्द').
claims.evidence: Both dictionaries the course relies on already record the compound. Apte 575a, under दूर: '-darśana, -dṛś a. far-seeing. -naḥ m. a vulture; a learned man. -naṃ prudence, foresight'. MW 489,3, dūra-darśana: m. 'far-seeing', a vulture (L.); n. 'long-sightedness, foresight' (W.); mfn. 'visible only from afar' (BhP. i, 11, 8). GRETIL texts have it too: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.11.8 'traiviṣṭapānām api dūradarśanam'; Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya on Pāśupatasūtra 5.13 'dūradarśanādayaḥ' (the yogic power of seeing far); Rājanighaṇṭu 19.103 'garutmān dūradarśanaḥ'. Only the sense 'television' is modern, as fact base 0.10 says; the compound itself is old. Q9 ('found ready-made with this meaning in classical texts') and Exercise 6 remain correct.
sources: Apte 1890 s.v. दूर (compound -darśana), p. 575a (Cologne AP90)
Monier-Williams 1899 s.v. dūra-darśana, p. 489,3 (Cologne MW)
Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.11.8, GRETIL e-text bhp_01u.htm
claims.correct_wording: दूरदर्शनम् 'television' is modern in this sense: a calque on tele-vision built from दूर 'far' and दर्शन 'seeing'. The compound itself is older, recorded as 'far-seeing; foresight' (Apte, MW). The course names no coiner and gives no date.

challenge.reason: I could not refute this. The problem is real but small. In l04, the Hindi in §7 says flatly "दूरदर्शनम् आधुनिक शब्द है". The vocabulary row and the §13 bullet say "MODERN" / "labelled modern". §8 sets दूरदर्शनम् (a calque) against विमानम् (an old word with a new job), which implies the compound did not exist before. The research behind fact 0.10 even says "A classical noun dūradarśana is NOT confirmed". That is wrong. MW s.v. दूर, which the §13 FACT callout already cites, lists dūra-darśana with older senses and a Bhāgavata Purāṇa citation. Apte 1890 p. 575a lists it, including the neuter noun "prudence, foresight". The compound is also used in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.11.8, Pāśupatasūtra-bhāṣya 5.13 and Rājanighaṇṭu 19.103. So only the sense "television" is modern. The proposed fixes are accurate and well hedged. All six quotes occur exactly once, and the validator passes after they are applied. Two changes are needed. First, the table cell's "(Apte, MW)" is not in the house citation format; it should read "(§13)", since the §13 FACT callout carries the [REF] tags. Second, a short note should go into the Exercise 6 key. Once the lesson says the compound is older, a student could defend the label "classical word, new sense" for दूरदर्शनम्.
challenge.better_wording: दूरदर्शनम् "television" is modern in this sense: a calque on *tele-vision* built from दूर "far" and दर्शन "seeing". The compound itself is older, recorded as "far-seeing; foresight" [REF:apte1890 s.v. दूर]; [REF:monierwilliams1899 s.v. दूर]. The course names no coiner and gives no date.

claims.decision_note: MW s.v. dūra-darśana confirms the older compound ('far-seeing', a vulture; n. long-sightedness, foresight).

claims.claim: सुखी comes from the stem सुखिन् 'having happiness'. It is a different word from the ledger's सुख, built like कुशली, and counts as ledger-new.
claims.evidence: Apte 1131a gives suKin a. 'Happy, glad, joyful'; MW 1222,1 gives sukhín 'possessing or causing happiness or pleasure, happy'. Whitney §1230 says possessive adjectives in -in are formed 'almost unlimitedly from stems in a'; §439 says the masculine nominative singular lengthens the i (balī). Pāṇini 5.2.115 अत इनिठनौ is the matching rule. The ledger glosses सुख 'happiness, ease' (v1.c04.l02 §14). So सुखी is a separate stem, not सुख in -ः or -म् dress, and counting it new follows STYLE_GUIDE §8 rules 1 and 3. One nuance: Apte 1130b and MW 1220,3 also list सुख as an adjective, 'happy, pleasant', whose masculine form would be सुखः. The lesson's 'happiness' versus 'happy' contrast therefore holds for the ledger's noun सुख.
sources: Apte 1890 s.vv. सुखिन्, p. 1131a, and सुख, p. 1130b
Monier-Williams 1899 s.vv. sukhin, p. 1222,1, and sukha, p. 1220,3

claims.claim: स्वपिति and गृह्णाति 'build their stems differently' (no root classes are named), and l02 §15's whole-word display rows स्वपिमि, स्वपिषि, गृह्णामि, गृह्णासि are correct.

Whitney §631 says svap inserts a 'union-vowel i before all the endings beginning with a consonant', giving 'svápimi'; Pāṇini 7.2.76 रुदादिभ्यः सार्वधातुके is the matching rule. The you-form is स्वपिषि because s becomes ṣ after i (Whitney §180). claims.claim: l02 §15 says the bank pattern would have given a wrong word ('स्वपिमि has no long आ before its -मि'), and calls this 'the whole reason these two are taught whole'.
claims.evidence: v2.c04.l02 §15 states the bank pattern as 'the front stays and the tail changes; in the -मि row the joint vowel stretches to आ' (for fronts in अ). Applied to the front गृह्णा- it gives गृह्णामि and गृह्णासि, which are the correct forms; the same happens with जाना-. Applied to स्वपि- it gives the correct स्वपिमि but the wrong 'स्वपिसि': the real form is स्वपिषि, with ष (Whitney §180). A learner who takes the front to be स्वप- gets 'स्वपामि', which is §12 mistake 1. So the pattern produces no wrong singular for गृह्णाति. The reason both verbs are taught whole is that their stems are built differently (Whitney §631; nā-class §717 ff.), and that shows most clearly beyond the singular (स्वपन्ति, गृह्णीमः).
sources: Sanskritam-Book v2.c04.l02 §15 FACT (2) and (5)
W.D. Whitney, A Sanskrit Grammar, 2nd ed. 1889, §§180, 631, 717
claims.correct_wording: गृह्णाति's row runs like जानाति's. स्वपिमि has no long आ, and its you-form स्वपिषि has ष, not स, so the bank pattern would give 'स्वपामि' or 'स्वपिसि'. Both stems are built differently, and more of that shows beyond the singular, which is why both are taught whole.

challenge.reason: The finding holds, though the problem is small. My strongest counter-argument fails. The course itself calls short-अ over-regularisation "the plain pattern bolted on": l02 §12 mistake 1 lists "गृह्णति", and c04.l02 §12 mistake 4 lists *जानसि and *जानमि. On that model the bank does mislead for गृह्णाति. But those errors only arise if the learner changes the front, which goes against "the front stays" (c04.l02 §15 FACT (2)) and against the method l02 §8 itself uses (build from the he-form, as with मुञ्चति). Taking the front गृह्णा- from गृह्णाति, the bank gives the correct गृह्णामि and गृह्णासि. That is exactly what the sentence's own "runs exactly like जानाति's" shows. So "the bank pattern would have given you a wrong word … That is the whole reason these two are taught whole" does not cover गृह्णाति. It also contradicts the lesson's own FACT (1), §7 and §8, which give the reason as stem-building. claims.evidence: मुञ्च and पश्य are 2sg active imperatives in which the bare thematic stem is the whole form (Whitney §544a). क्षमस्व is the 2sg middle imperative of क्षमते, with the ending -स्व (Whitney §544b). v2.c01.l04 §8 calls it 'a classical imperative of √क्षम्'. challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The line is loose rather than flatly false, but the problem is real. When this course talks about the "shape" of a word, it means its surface form. The same lesson's §14 row for मुञ्च says only "the पश्य shape (§8)". The course also teaches learners to read verbs by their tails. मुञ्च and पश्य share a shape: both are the bare present stem used as the you-form imperative. क्षमस्व is the same mood and person, but it carries the middle ending -स्व, so it does not share that shape.

The strongest counter-reading takes "shape" to mean "the त्वम्-form", echoing v2.c05.l02 §16 ("क्षमस्व ... is itself a त्वम्-form"). The fix keeps that point as "the same mood and person". It also keeps "the shape of पश्य", which the §14 pointer depends on. The proposed wording is accurate. Its quote occurs exactly once. It adds no IAST parenthesis, IPA or REF, and the validator gives 0 errors and 0 warnings before and after the change.

It does not reopen the course's rule for chunks. v2.c05.l03 already points at a tail on a word taught whole (रोचते "-ते, not -ति"). The fix names an ending but builds no paradigm and does not tell learners to split the word when they use it. One optional improvement, not required: say that -स्व belongs to the other ending family, the middle voice that रोचते wears (v2.c05.l03). That would stop learners from treating -स्व as a free alternative ending.

claims.claim: l02 §8 FACT says 'निद्राम् करोति "makes sleep" is not the classical idiom for it', and fact base 0.4 calls the phrase unidiomatic.

challenge.reason:
The researcher's attestations are real, but they do not show that the lesson overclaims, and the proposed fix has problems of its own.

1. The l02 §8 FACT says निद्राम् करोति is "not the classical idiom for it". It does not say the phrase is unattested. The researcher's own result ("rare and late, not the usual way to say it") says the same thing. The dictionaries back it:
   - PWG s.v. nidrā lists the classical verbs used with nidrām: sev, abhi-i, upa-gam, gam, yā, upa-i, labh, pra-āp, vah, vi-hā, tyaj. It has no kṛ.
   - Apte's English–Sanskrit dictionary, s.v. Sleep, gives svap, śī, saṃviś, ni-drā and "go to sleep: nidrāṃ yā". It has no nidrāṃ kṛ.
   - Where an earlier text has nidrāṃ … kurute, it means "causes drowsiness", not "sleeps" (Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya Utt. 37.50; MW's nidrā-kara "making sleepy", Hariv., Suśr.). So the course's gloss "makes sleep" is apt.
   - Two of the four cited texts use special senses: Narmamālā 2.65 is feigned sleep (mudhaiva), and Śiva Purāṇa 7.1.11.16 is yogic sleep.
   The student-facing FACT is accurate as written, and no quiz item tests it.

2. The proposed lesson wording adds a claim about textual history ("rare and late (some later texts have it)") to a FACT callout. The callout's references (apte1890 s.vv. स्वप्, ग्रह्, मुच्, कृत्; monierwilliams1899 s.v. kṛt) do not support that claim; the researcher concedes that Apte and MW do not record the phrase. REFERENCES.md has no key for GRETIL, the Tantrāloka or the Narmamālā, and the proposal adds no new_references. That breaks EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES §2. The wording also calls the phrase glossed "makes sleep" "late", though the "causes sleep" sense is found earlier.

3. Fix 3 says "not in the critical-edition Mahābhārata", which is imprecise. The critical-edition e-text prints Appendix I passage 31 (after 1.55.3), which has the passive of the same idiom: "naiva nidrā kāryā". Only the constituted text lacks it. The replacement also keeps 'निद्राम् करोति ("makes sleep")', an English gloss in a parenthesis straight after Devanagari, which the house rule reserves for IAST.

4. The researcher missed one source. MW's English–Sanskrit dictionary (1851) does list nidrāṃ kṛ under "To SLEEP" and "To DOZE"; the original evidence file had flagged this as unchecked. It is a composition dictionary without citations. It makes the internal note's word "unidiomatic" look somewhat strong, but it does not affect the lesson.

At most the internal note 0.4 could be reworded for precision. That is optional, the finding's main claim against the lesson fails, and the default when uncertain is not upheld.

The problem is real. Classical Sanskrit fable books have animals addressing each other with भवान् as well as त्वम्, sometimes both in one speech. So "Animals in fables address each other as त्वम्, so the mouse uses it to the lion" wrongly presents the choice as the fable convention. The Hindi is worse: "तुम कहकर ही" says "only तुम". The researcher's proposal is right in substance, but its fixes need two changes. (1) Fix 2 produces "त्वम् (fable animals also say भवान् to each other)". That puts a prose aside in a parenthesis directly after a Devanagari word, which breaks the house rule that such a parenthesis holds only that word's IAST. (2) The Hindi fix drops the भवान् caveat, so §7 and §8 would no longer say the same thing. The better fixes below drop the parenthesis, keep the two explanations parallel, and cite the existing hitopadesha key, using the "mitralābha" locator that §4 of this lesson already uses.

In India's old fable books, animals address each other both ways, as त्वम् and as भवान् [REF:hitopadesha mitralābha]." claims.claim: l01 §4 FACT: 'एकः काकः अस्ति "there is a crow" is graded-reader Sanskrit: correct, and normal in readers for learners. Classical storytellers usually mark "a certain one" with an indefinite word such as कश्चित् (kaścit), and often tell the tale in a past tense — आसीत्.'
claims.evidence: The callout cites Whitney without a section, and Whitney §482c says the opposite of its contrast: 'In the late literature, eka is used in the sense of a certain, or even sometimes almost of a, as an indefinite article. Thus, eko vyāghraḥ (H.) a certain tiger'. In the GRETIL Hitopadeśa, the prose after 1.5 has 'apaśyam eko vṛddho vyāghraḥ'. The prastāvikā opens 'asti bhāgīrathī-tīre pāṭaliputra-nāmadheyaṃ nagaram | tatra ... sudarśano nāma narapatir āsīt', and 22 tales open with asti 'there is'. Present-tense narration is normal: the prose after 1.55 has 'mṛga-kākau nivasataḥ', and elsewhere 'parivrājakaḥ prativasati'. कश्चित् occurs 19 times. So the course's opening, एकः with अस्ति and present-tense narration, is close to classical fable prose. Calling it 'graded-reader Sanskrit', in contrast to what classical storytellers 'usually' do, overstates the gap. The core is true: कश्चित् and past-tense narration are both common.
sources: W.D. Whitney, A Sanskrit Grammar, 2nd ed. 1889, §§482, 507
Nārāyaṇa, Hitopadeśa, GRETIL e-text hitop_u.htm (prastāvikā opening; Mitralābha prose after 1.5 and 1.55)
claims.correct_wording: एकः काकः अस्ति 'there is a crow' is correct Sanskrit and close to classical fable prose. The Hitopadeśa opens its tales with अस्ति 'there is', and later prose can use एक itself for 'a certain'. Storytellers also mark 'a certain one' with कश्चित्, and often tell the tale in a past tense such as आसीत्.

challenge.reason:
The original callout's literal claims are hedged and hold up against the primary texts. The sentence is correct, and normal in learners' readers. Classical storytellers do usually mark "a certain one" with a kaścit-form: in the Hitopadeśa these outnumber eka used for "a certain" by about 6 to 1, and in the Pañcatantra by far more. They also often tell the tale in a past tense; the classical texts typically bring in their characters with āsīt, babhūva or prativasati sma. Whitney §482c does say that eka means "a certain" in the late literature, "sometimes almost" "a". But it calls this a late usage that happens "sometimes", so it adds a nuance; it does not "say the opposite". The researcher's own passages support the original. The prose after Hit 1.55 goes on: "kenacit śṛgālenāvalokitaḥ … 'cintayat … abravīt". That is a kaścit indefinite followed by past tenses; only the setting verb nivasataḥ is present. The prastāvikā, cited in the proposal, brings in its king with "sudarśano nāma narapatir āsīt", which is the original's "āsīt, 'there was'".

The proposal has its own problems:
(1) "Close to classical fable prose" overclaims the other way. Classical openings put asti first, then a place and a name or kaścit-form, and tell the events in a past tense. The course tells every event in the present.
(2) "Opens its tales with asti" needs "most of".
(3) "Storytellers also mark … with कश्चित्" demotes the usual marker.
(4) [REF:hitopadesha prastāvikā] covers one opening only, and that opening uses āsīt for its character.
(5) Whitney §507 (kaścit) is not cited.
(6) Line 175, "Both are display only", loses its referent once अस्ति and एक appear in the callout.
(7) The proposed wording and the fixes do not match.

The three quotes each occur exactly once, and the REF keys exist. Separately, the bare [REF:whitney1889] still lacks a locator. The lesson's own Pass C flag already tracks this, and §§482, 507 would fit. That is a different issue from the claimed overclaim.

claims.decision_note: Skeptic not upheld: the l01 FACT on एकः काकः अस्ति is hedged and holds against the primary texts.

claims.claim: l02 §11 check 4 calls the vowel of कृन्तति a 'curl-free ऋ'.
claims.evidence: Volume 1 teaches the opposite. v1.c02.l03 §11 says: 'Tongue: tip up and lightly curled toward the ridge just behind the upper teeth ... Think "resting at the tap position"'. That is the course's model for /r̩/ (STYLE_GUIDE §2: syllabic r). This is minor, but 'curl-free' contradicts it.
sources: Sanskritam-Book v1.c02.l03 §11; STYLE_GUIDE.md §2.1

challenge.reason:
I could not refute the finding. The strongest defence is this: from v1.c03.l03 on, the course uses "curl" for the retroflex gesture ("curl the tip back and tap the dome"), and check 2 in this same §11 uses it that way for ण. On that reading, "curl-free ऋ" would just mean "not retroflex", which fits the alveolar tap-position model. That defence fails because Volume 2 itself describes ऋ as a curl:
- v2.c02.l03 §9 drill 2 says "/r̩/, tongue curled".
- v2.c02.l03 §11 check 1 says "the tongue tip curls up and holds".
- v2.c04.l01 §11, under the heading "The curl check (शृणोति)", says "The tongue tip curls twice — once for ृ … once for ण".

A learner who has done those checks is now told that ऋ is "curl-free". That is a real contradiction, and it is wider than the researcher reported, because it covers Volume 2 as well as v1.c02.l03 §11 ("tip up and lightly curled toward the ridge"). From my own knowledge, the traditional place list (ऋटुरषाणां मूर्धा) puts ṛ among the mūrdhanya sounds, so "curl-free" is not supported by tradition either. I could not check that against a source, because no web search ran.

The proposed wording is correct:
- "ऋ at the tap position" is the course's own established model. It appears in the v1.c02.l03 §5 FACT callout ("the tongue takes the position of the tap r", cited to [REF:whitney1889 §24] and [REF:ladefoged2015]), in §8 step 1, in §9 drill 1 rung 4, in §11 and in §20.
- It matches v1.c04.l01 ("you held /r̩/ at the ridge") and Volume 2's "tip curls up and holds".
- It matches this lesson's own §9 drill 1 ("कृन्तति (ऋ, then न्त at the teeth)").
- It keeps the contrast with check 2: ridge, then teeth, so the tongue never goes back to the dome.
- It adds no new claim that would need a REF.

The quote occurs exactly once. The replacement is NFC-clean and keeps the house rules: no Devanagari-plus-parenthesis, IPA unchanged, no callout, no quotation marks.

The problem is real, and the course's own Chapter 4 text shows it. The l05 §17 footnote says "Every verb is built by the Chapter 4 pattern … each with the stretch to -आमि". But the I-form story uses अस्मि three times (twice in line 1, once in line 6), and v2.c04.l02 §15 says outright that the trio अस्मि · असि · अस्ति must be learned whole: "it is the model for the pattern, not an application of it — no joint vowel to stretch". The pattern itself is stated only for the regular bank (गच्छ- … हस-). In grammar terms, अस्मि is a root-class form, as-mi, so it never takes the -आमि stretch. Line 6's अस्मि also replaces l01's भवति, so it is not even the I-form of the original verb. Line 3 keeps the he-form अस्ति (घटे अल्पम् जलम् अस्ति), which "Line 5 keeps one he-form" leaves out. Second, use more natural Hindi tied to Chapter 4's own term पहचान-त्रयी. Third, add a matching fix to the §27 policy audit, which repeats the overclaim ("the 1sg crow built by the c04 pattern").

claims.claim: l03 §16 and §17 line 6 translate उद्यमः बलम् into Hindi as 'उद्यम ही बल है'.
claims.evidence: The Sanskrit उद्यमः बलम् has no एव, and Hindi ही is the course's own rendering of एव (बुद्धिः एव बलम् becomes बुद्धि ही बल है). l03 §6 glosses the same Sanskrit as 'उद्यम बल है।', and the English everywhere is 'Effort is strength'.
sources: Sanskritam-Book v2.c06.l03 §6; v2.c06.l01 §17 (बुद्धि ही बल है)
claims.correct_wording: उद्यमः बलम् — उद्यम बल है।

challenge.reason:
The problem is real. Lesson 3 translates its own Sanskrit line उद्यमः बलम् into Hindi two different ways. §6 has 'उद्यम बल है।'. §16 and §17 line 6 have 'उद्यम ही बल है'.

The ही version adds an emphatic, restrictive particle that the Sanskrit does not have (there is no एव or हि). The English in all three places is plain 'Effort is strength'. This same chapter teaches ही as the Hindi for एव: l01 renders बुद्धिः एव बलम् as 'बुद्धि ही बल है', and its Hindi note says एव puts weight on the word before it. Volume 1 does the same, rendering सत्यम् एव जयते as 'सत्य ही जीतता है'.

Inside §16 and §17, the matching verbless line परोपकारः पुण्यम् is rendered 'परोपकार पुण्य है' with no ही, so उद्यमः बलम् is the only line that gets one. A reader of the Hindi alone (the Pass B check) would translate it back as उद्यमः एव बलम्. That blurs the plain-versus-एव contrast that l01 §8 draws on purpose, and that l03 §6 and §17 point to when they call the line 'shaped like' बुद्धिः एव बलम्.

The counter-arguments fail:
- (a) ही sounds natural in a Hindi maxim, but it is not needed. §6 of this lesson already uses the plain form, and so does the matching परोपकार line.
- (b) The one other place the course adds ही without एव is v1.c05.l03 (ज्ञानम् बलम् → 'ज्ञान ही बल है'). That conflicts with l01 §8, which treats ज्ञानम् बलम् as the form with no emphasis word, so it looks like the same slip in another chapter rather than a rule. The researcher's statement that ही is the course's rendering of एव still holds.

The fix is correct:
- Each quote occurs exactly once in the lesson file (checked as an exact NFC string).
- The replacements copy §6's wording word for word and keep the four-layer format, with the Hindi as plain Devanagari and no quotes.
- A patched copy run through scripts/validate.py in a scratchpad mirror of the repo gave 0 errors and 0 warnings.

Process note: after applying the fix, regenerate json/volume-2/v2.c06.l03.json with `python3 scripts/export_json.py`. With the patched lesson in place, `export_json.py --check` reports that file as out of date. This is the normal regeneration step, not a flaw in the fix. Optional follow-up outside this chapter: the v1.c05.l03 §6 Hindi has the same issue.

challenge.reason:
I could not refute it. The problem is real. In §17 the snake (line 1) and the aeroplane (line 3) speak in feminine Hindi (मैं चलती हूँ, मैं ऊपर जाती हूँ), but the television and the tooth (lines 5 and 7) speak in the masculine. The craft note justifies the masculine only by how Hindi genders the object ("as Hindi speaks of टेलीविज़न and दाँत"). That reason applies just as much to साँप and हवाई जहाज़, which are both masculine. The lesson's own Hindi also makes साँप masculine with the same verb: §6 has साँप चलता है। and §16 has साँप चल रहा है। वह चूहा चाहता है! So the snake's मैं चलती हूँ contradicts the lesson itself. Pass B in EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES requires a gender and agreement check, and this fails it.

The text gives no sign that lines 1 and 3 are माया speaking as herself. Those lines are said by the thing being guessed: it has no foot, goes up high and is not a crow. Treating them as her own (female) voice would also clash with lines 5 and 7, so the inconsistency stays either way. The feminine even points a Hindi reader toward feminine answers, which works against the riddles.

The proposal is correct and minimal: change चलती to चलता and जाती to जाता, and extend the note to all four lines. Each fix quote occurs exactly once. The patched lesson passes the validator. The new note is accurate, needs no IAST, REF or register callout, and stays within the file's 90-character line width. The Sanskrit is unaffected, because finite present-tense verbs (चलामि, गच्छामि) carry no gender. The proposed summary wording is accurate once the fix is applied.

The text is as the researcher says: l05 §13 renders sentence 6 as "एक दिन शेर / जाल में बँध जाता है।" (lines 424–425), while its own English gloss on line 418 says "One day the lion is caught in a net." The course renders this exact sentence with फँस everywhere else, four times in l02. One of those is §7, which EDITORIAL_GUIDELINES describes as Hindi "written natively". l02 §14 also pairs "caught" with "फँसा हुआ". The defence that बँध is a literal rendering of बद्धः ("bound", l05 §14 "बँधा हुआ") does not hold, because the rest of this Hindi paragraph is idiomatic rather than literal: it says जंगल, merges sentences with क्रोधित होकर, and writes मुक्त और सुखी हो जाता है. In idiomatic Hindi a net traps you (जाल में फँसना); बँधना means being tied, as with a rope or a bond. So this is a real but minor Pass B natural-register issue, and the line also breaks consistency with l02. The proposed wording matches l02 §17 line 8 word for word. The fix quote occurs exactly once. challenge.reason:
The finding shows no error, and the proposal would make the lesson worse.

(1) The text is not shown to be wrong or overclaimed. The researcher concedes these are "standard Indo-Aryan etymologies". Their "unverifiable" verdict describes the session's tools, not the text. I could not reach a source either, so nothing contradicts the text. It matches the standard derivations: danta > Prakrit daṃta > Hindi dā̃t; sarpa > Prakrit sappa > Hindi sā̃p; pāda > Prakrit pāa > Hindi pā̃v. These are Turner's CDIAL headwords dánta, pā́da and sarpá. तद्भव is the ordinary Hindi-grammar term for exactly this class of word, and these three are stock textbook pairs.

(2) The missing citation breaks no house rule. None of the 30 Volume 2 §7 sections carries a REF tag. The reviewed lesson v2.c02.l02 makes an uncited descent claim of the same strength in its §7 ("बहन इसी शब्द की सीधी वंशज है, प्राकृत की सीढ़ियों से उतरती"). Its matching §27 flag ("बहन ← भगिनी descent (§7, §22) against [REF:masica1991]") was closed by verification (logged ✅ with masica1991), not by softening. गृह → घर and क्षेत्र → खेत were closed the same way. The open Pass C flag is already in l04 §27, so the finding adds nothing new.

(3) The proposal is not correct for this lesson.
(a) "Everyday Hindi relatives" blurs the distinction the lesson teaches. In §7 the kinship words already belong to other kinds: सजातीय = "एक ही पुरखे की सन्तानें", the Latin-route words are "चचेरे भाई", and juggle is "*joke* का रिश्तेदार". Calling the Hindi words "relatives" would group these inherited words with the cousins and with juggle/joke, and lose the direction of inheritance. The lesson's objective is honesty about direction.
(b) An "uncited present-day bridge" would offer the words on resemblance alone. The sentence just before says "आवाज़ का मिलना सबूत नहीं होता — सबूत होता है नियम से दोहराया जाने वाला ध्वनि-मेल".
(c) The proposal is conditional ("once checked … otherwise soften"), names no checked locus and has no fixes, so there is nothing to apply.
(d) A turner1966 key is reasonable in principle as a later, more precise addition. It is not needed to close a flag the house closes with masica1991, and it cannot honestly be added until someone actually reads the entries.

Recommended resolution, which needs no text change: keep §7 and §22 as written. Close the §27 flag in Pass C by checking Turner s.vv. dánta, pā́da, sarpá (or Masica 1991) once a reference host can be reached, and log the result as a verification-log row. Soften only if that check fails.
